Foundation examination: Volumes1–4Economics core examinationFinance core examination

Author-reviewed

Cumulative assessment · Volumes 7–11

Finance core: accounts, value, investment and institutions

Defend a financial decision from the transaction that creates a claim to the date on which someone must fund it. Reconcile reported performance, economic value, portfolio risk and actual settlement before recommending an action.

This package follows the accepted chapter and assessment work in accounting, corporate finance, investments, fixed income and derivatives and banking and institutional risk. Its cases require connections across those subjects. It samples essential capabilities; it does not retest every result in all sixty chapters or establish a learner’s professional authorization.

Administration and evidence of mastery

Complete the diagnostic before either written form. Attempt Form A first and reserve Form B for reassessment after correcting the mechanisms behind any errors. Each form contains five 20-point domains, for 100 points. Work without notes, code, internet access or solutions; a nonprogrammable calculator and blank paper are allowed. Suggested time is 300 minutes per form. That is an author’s planning estimate, not a measured completion time or evidence that the forms are statistically equated. A grader may arrange accommodations and record the actual administration conditions.

All case quantities, probabilities, prices, rights and funding commitments are original teaching assumptions unless explicitly identified otherwise. Do not import a country’s tax treatment, accounting rule, deposit guarantee, insolvency power or market convention into an explicitly stipulated contract. Identify the date, currency, owner, availability and priority of each resource. If a required action needs a new source of money or permission, name it and recompute the affected claims.

The practical is open resource. Produce an independent analysis and implementation before examining its supplied reference output or instructor guide. A working benchmark is a comparison tool; executing it does not demonstrate that you can reconstruct the accounts, justify the valuation or detect a model’s unsuitable use. Retain your original submission, corrections, input provenance and explanation of changed conclusions.

  • Written advancement: at least 85/100 overall and 15/20 in each domain, followed by satisfactory unfamiliar transfer and teach-back. Use the same criterion for reassessment, with a fresh attempt rather than editing the first response while reading the answer.
  • Practical advancement: at least 85/100, at least 15/20 in each of its five essential domains, reproducible evidence, and a defensible response to the assigned transfer. A plausible recommendation alone is insufficient.
  • Critical errors: invented cash or authority; deleting a surviving claim; treating a financing inflow as operating profit; inconsistent cash flow and discount rate; substituting physical probabilities for pricing weights without justification; spending collateral twice; funding an earlier payment with an unbridged later receipt; presenting a fitted model as independently validated; or altering evidence to conceal a failure. Correct each such error and pass a new transfer before advancement, regardless of total score.
  • Grading: carry a transparent arithmetic error through consistent later work without repeatedly deducting for it. Deduct separately for a new conceptual error. Accept an alternative recommendation when its original-contract calculations are correct and its changed assumptions, funding, rights and trade-offs are explicit. Do not award points merely for reproducing the instructor’s policy preference.

These thresholds are the library’s criterion-based design. They are neither admissions requirements nor a credential. Research originality, investment skill, observed teaching and real institutional judgment require evidence and independent human evaluation beyond completing these synthetic assessments.

Five essential domains and their connections

DomainRequired reasoningA connection that must survive the calculation
D1 · Accounts and operating evidenceReconcile transactions, accrual income, operating cash and estimates; identify the claim behind an entry.An allowance changes carrying value without supplying cash; a forecast must reconcile its financing requirement.
D2 · Value and financingChoose incremental cash flows, consistent discounting and the correct enterprise-to-claim bridge.Debt face, debt proceeds, ownership dilution, book equity and economic value have different meanings.
D3 · Investment and evidenceSeparate physical risk from claim pricing, solve a feasible allocation problem and assess implementation or performance evidence.A return target or fitted premium does not remove covariance uncertainty, costs, liabilities or trading constraints.
D4 · Fixed income and hedgingDerive dated claim values or replicating positions and explain residual risk.An ideal payoff hedge can still need collateral funding or suffer delayed counterparty recovery.
D5 · Institutions and decisionsReconcile liquidity, solvency, seniority and a coherent stress response; state who can act and who bears loss.Positive value, a cash injection, a changed legal claim and effective operational delivery are separate propositions.

The domain scores support diagnosis; they do not imply that a question belongs to only one volume. A funded acquisition, for example, may require all five domains. The examinations identify the outcomes they sample, and the practical combines them in one documented decision.

Prerequisite diagnostic · 40 points

Suggested time: 60 minutes, under the written-form resource rules. Each item is worth five points. Attempt all eight before opening the solutions. Advance to the written form at 34/40 or higher, with at least four points each on items 1, 2, 6 and 7, and no unresolved critical error. Otherwise use the remediation routes below and take a changed version of the failed mechanism.

  1. Profit and actual cash. A fictional company records revenue 100 CU and collects 80 CU. Gross receivables begin at 15 and end at 35. Cash operating expenses are 55 and depreciation is 10. There are no other expenses, accruals, taxes or interest. Cash begins at 12; the company pays capital expenditure 20, receives new borrowing 8 and pays a dividend 5. Compute income, operating cash flow and closing cash. Show why neither the borrowing nor capital expenditure belongs in this period’s stated income calculation.
  2. The claim being valued. EBIT is 40 CU, the stipulated unlevered cash tax rate is 25%, depreciation is 8, capital expenditure is 15 and the increase in operating net working capital is 5. Financing interest of 4 is reported separately. Compute FCFF. An independently justified operating enterprise value is supplied as 180; debt market value is 50 and unrestricted surplus cash is 10. Compute equity value and explain why one period’s FCFF does not, by itself, establish the supplied enterprise value.
  3. A funded total return. A share costs 80 CU, pays a dividend of 4 during the holding period and ends at 88. For this exercise the dividend is held as cash without interest; there are no fees or intermediate contributions. A separate portfolio begins with 100: 60 invested in this stock return and 40 in a bond with total return −5%. Compute the stock’s total return, each holding’s final wealth, and the portfolio’s total return. Do not add the dividend a second time.
  4. Two kinds of weights. In a complete one-date, two-state teaching market, Arrow claims paying one CU in states U and D cost 0.4 and 0.5 CU respectively. Physical probabilities are 0.7 and 0.3. Price a claim paying 20 in U and zero in D, compute its physical expected payoff, and derive the gross return on a traded claim paying one in both states. Explain why the two claim quantities differ.
  5. Dates on a curve. A bond pays 5 CU at date 1 and 105 at date 2. The matching zero-coupon discount factors are 0.96 and 0.90, with no credit loss or transaction costs. Compute its full price and the net forward rate for the one-period interval from date 1 to date 2. State the investment comparison that establishes that forward rate.
  6. Replication, including its debt. A stock costs 50 CU and will be worth either 65 or 40 at the next date. It pays no dividend. The bank account has gross return 1.05; borrowing and lending at this rate, fractional shares and the required short positions are permitted without frictions. A European call has strike 50. Derive the stock holding, initial bank position and call price. Verify the terminal portfolio in both states and state the risk-neutral up probability implied by these traded assets.
  7. A valuable firm can miss a payment. A firm has assets 200 CU, liabilities 170 and equity 30. Its assets include usable cash 4 and a receivable of 12 that will be paid only after an obligation of 9 is due. No other resource arrives at that first cutoff. An outside lender has five CU of separate available cash and offers to deliver five before the obligation; repayment 5.5 is due after the receivable is collected. Compute the initial payment gap and the two cash balances if the bridge is executed and all stated payments occur. Explain the effect of collecting the receivable on income.
  8. The first cash flow in a terminal value. A complete perpetual contract pays FCFF of 12 CU at date 1, then grows that payment by 2% each year forever. The appropriate constant annual discount rate is 8%. There are no separate terminal assets or additional cash flows. Compute the continuation value immediately after the date-1 payment and the total value at date 0. Explain the convergence condition and where the date-1 cash enters.
Diagnostic solutions and five-point rubrics
  1. Income 35; operating cash 25; closing cash 20 CU. Income is 100−55−10=35. Operating cash is receipts less paid expenses, 80−55=25; equivalently 35+10−(35−15)=25. Capital expenditure is an asset investment under the stipulated accounts; depreciation, rather than the whole purchase, is the current expense. Borrowing creates an equal cash asset and financing liability, not revenue. Closing cash is 12+25−20+8−5=20. Receivables reconcile as 15+100−80=35. Credit five: income one; operating cash and receivable bridge two; closing cash one; correct investment/financing classification one.
  2. FCFF 18; equity value 140 CU. Unlevered after-tax operating income is 40(1−0.25)=30. FCFF=30+8−15−5=18. Financing interest is excluded from this cash flow available before distributions to capital providers; subtracting it here while using an enterprise discounting approach would change the object being valued. Equity=180+10−50=140 because surplus cash is outside the supplied operating value and debt is another claim on the combined resources. A value needs the relevant future cash-flow path, risk and discounting assumptions; a single observed 18 does not supply them. Credit five: FCFF computation two; interest treatment one; enterprise/equity bridge one; limitation of a single period one.
  3. Stock return 15%; closing wealth 69 and 38; portfolio return 7%. The stock delivers 88+4=92 on an initial 80, so its total return is 12/80=0.15. The stock allocation ends at 60(1.15)=69, already including its proportionate dividend; the bond ends at 40(0.95)=38. Total final wealth is 107 and the funded return is (107−100)/100=0.07. Equivalently 0.6(0.15)+0.4(−0.05)=0.07. This is a one-period total return under the specified dividend convention, not a time-weighted attribution for an account with outside flows. Credit five: stock return one; two terminal holdings two; portfolio return one; correct dividend/contribution treatment one.
  4. Price 8; physical expected payoff 14 CU; risk-free gross return 10/9. Replicating the claim requires twenty U Arrow claims, costing 20(0.4)=8. Its physical mean is 0.7(20)+0.3(0)=14. One claim in each state costs 0.4+0.5=0.9 and pays one surely, giving gross return 1/0.9=10/9. State prices combine discounting and the price of state-contingent delivery; physical weights describe the assumed frequencies. Multiplying the physical mean by an arbitrary discount factor is not a substitute for the specified market’s replicating price. Credit five: price one; physical mean one; sure claim and gross return two; interpretation one.
  5. Price 99.3 CU; net forward rate 1/15, approximately 6.6667%. Value each date separately: 5(0.96)+105(0.90)=4.8+94.5=99.3. The no-arbitrage gross forward factor is D(0,1)/D(0,2)=0.96/0.90=16/15; subtract one to get 1/15. Buying one date-1 CU now costs 0.96; agreeing to reinvest that CU at the forward rate must deliver the same date-2 amount that 0.96 buys directly in the date-2 zero, namely 0.96/0.90. A yield to maturity is not supplied or needed. Credit five: dated price two; forward factor and net rate two; matched-date investment argument one.
  6. Hold 3/5 of a share and a bank position −160/7 CU; call price 50/7 CU. The payoff difference is 15−0 across a stock difference 65−40=25, so Δ=3/5. In the down state the stock delivers 24 and the bank must deliver −24; its initial position is −24/1.05=−160/7. Initial portfolio value is (3/5)50−160/7=50/7. At maturity it delivers 39−24=15 in U and 24−24=0 in D. The implied up weight satisfies 50(1.05)=65q+40(1−q), giving q=1/2; discounting its expected call payoff gives the same 50/7. No physical probability is needed. Credit five: stock position one; initial bank amount one; price one; both state cash checks one; implied pricing weight one.
  7. Early gap five; funded cash zero at the first cutoff and 6.5 later. Positive equity 30 does not change 9−4=5 unavailable at the deadline. The lender’s actual five gives 4+5−9=0 after paying the obligation. Later, collection 12 and bridge repayment 5.5 leave 6.5. The lender supplies cash from its stated endowment and receives principal plus 0.5 interest; the bridge is a new claim with a later maturity. Collection exchanges the receivable for cash and is not another twelve of revenue; the 0.5 bridge interest is a financing expense under the stated transaction. Credit five: deadline gap one; dated balances two; new funded liability/interest one; collection classification one.
  8. Continuation at date 1 is 204; value at date 0 is 200 CU. The first payment belonging to the continuation is date-2 cash 12(1.02)=12.24. Immediately after receiving date-1 cash, the remaining stream is worth 12.24/(0.08−0.02)=204. Hence date-0 value is (12+204)/1.08=200, also 12/(0.08−0.02). The discounted geometric ratio 1.02/1.08 is below one, so the infinite sum converges. The date-1 payment is included once outside its after-payment continuation; including it again inside that continuation would double count. The contract fixes growth and discounting forever, a strong assumption to challenge in a real valuation. Credit five: correct continuation numerator/date one; continuation value one; present value one; convergence condition one; correct first-payment accounting one.

Repair the failed mechanism

Diagnostic evidenceRead and reconstructFresh check before retrying
1 · Cash and income disagreeTransactions, three statements and working capital.Change collection timing while holding recognized revenue fixed; reconcile both receivables and cash.
2 or 8 · Cash flow/value mismatchFCFF and FCFE, terminal assumptions and enterprise/equity comparisons.Identify exactly which future stream is included, change reinvestment or growth, and avoid counting surplus cash twice.
3 or 4 · Return/probability confusionTotal returns, portfolio mathematics and state prices.Alter physical probabilities while holding traded state prices fixed; distinguish the changed expectation from the unchanged price.
5 or 6 · Missing dated hedge cashDiscount curves, forwards and collateral and finite replication.Write every stock, debt and derivative payment by date and state, then change one financing term.
7 · Value substituted for fundingCapital and liquidity, dated funding and currency and claim access.Delay the bridge or restrict the receivable’s location; compute the earliest actual payment failure.

Form A — Juniper's growth plan, investors and payment network

This original 100-point, closed-resource examination contains five 20-point cases. Suggested time is 300 minutes, an uncalibrated planning estimate. Use a nonprogrammable calculator and blank paper; no notes, code, internet or solutions. Exact fractions or correctly labeled approximations earn credit. All amounts are in fictional currency units, CU. Dates, taxes, accounting policies, trading rights, prices and counterparty resources are stipulated teaching assumptions; no actual company, market observation or national legal rule is asserted.

The cases follow an operating company, a prospective investor and a treasury intermediary, but each restates its own complete information at a separate decision date. Do not carry a cash balance, stock price or interest rate from one case into another. State what is owned, owed, priced and usable before making a recommendation. An answer about value does not substitute for a funded payment. Required methods are taught in the accepted Volume 7–11 chapters; the coverage table identifies the particular outcomes sampled.

Five essential domains; 20 points each
CaseSampled outcomes and method routesSubpart points
1 · Reported operationsDouble entry, statement reconciliation, working capital, asset carrying amounts and earnings evidence.6 + 8 + 6
2 · Growth and ownershipIncremental investment, FCFF, financing claims, new equity ownership and capital allocation.7 + 8 + 5
3 · An investor's objective and evidenceFunded total returns, state prices, performance evaluation, expected utility and mandate limits.8 + 5 + 7
4 · A contingent payment and its financingDated discounting, funding and collateral, finite dynamic replication and model-use conditions.8 + 6 + 6
5 · A funded institutional responseCapital versus cash, deadlines, execution evidence, joint clearing, network transmission and accountable decisions.6 + 6 + 8

The form samples connected capabilities rather than every result in sixty chapters. Advancement requires at least 85/100 overall and 15/20 in each domain, followed by satisfactory unfamiliar transfer and teach-back. Critical errors in accounting, units, claim ownership, funding, double counting or integrity require remediation even if the total passes. These are authored library criteria, not calibrated form equivalence or a credential. Carry a transparent arithmetic slip through consistent subsequent work without repeated deductions; assess a new conceptual error separately.

Case 1 — Cash from a customer is not always earned revenue

At the beginning of a reporting period Juniper Components has the following accounts. There are no omitted accounts, taxes, new capital expenditures, new borrowings or changes in ownership during this period. Interest paid is classified as operating cash flow under the stipulated policy; principal repayment and dividends are financing flows.

Opening balance sheet, CU
AssetsAmountLiabilities and equityAmount
Cash15Trade payables18
Trade receivables20Unearned customer advances10
Inventory at carrying cost30Debt principal40
Net property, plant and equipment80Equity77

Regular goods sales create credit revenue of 160; collections against opening and current receivables total 150. Customers separately pay 12 in advance for goods not delivered by period end. Juniper also delivers goods satisfying eight of the opening ten of customer advances; recognize revenue of eight and extinguish that amount of the contract liability. No cash is collected again for those deliveries. All goods delivered, including those covered by the eight released advances, are included in the stated goods-consumed cost below.

Inventory purchases of 100 are all on trade credit. Goods delivered consume inventory carrying cost 90. A supported end-period estimate requires an additional inventory write-down of six, charged to expense; it is not a cash payment. Supplier payments are 95. Cash wages are 30, depreciation is 12, cash interest is four, debt principal repaid is five, and the dividend paid is six. All cash receipts come from the named customers; payments go to suppliers, employees, the debt holder and shareholders as indicated. Cash and accrued amounts are distinct.

  1. Recognition and closing operating accounts. State the entries for the new customer advance, release of the old advance and inventory write-down. Derive closing receivables, inventory, trade payables and unearned advances.
  2. Reconcile the statements. Compute income, operating cash flow by both the direct and an indirect method, closing cash, closing net PPE, debt, equity and the complete closing balance-sheet totals. Show that borrowing principal and dividends have not been charged as operating expenses.
  3. Challenge the report. An analyst recognizes the new 12 advance as additional current revenue and omits the six inventory write-down. The analyst leaves the eight legitimately earned advance release in revenue. Quantify the resulting income and equity overstatement, explain whether this changes actual period cash, and identify two concrete pieces of evidence needed before using the corrected income or operating cash as a recurring forecast.

Case 2 — A positive project and a fair share of it

At a separate planning date, Juniper can build one additional production line. Rejecting it leaves the status quo unchanged. At date 0 it pays an equipment vendor 60 and invests ten in operating working capital, paid to a separate inventory supplier. Equipment depreciates by 30 at each of dates 1 and 2 and has no final sale value. The line has no effect on legacy operations. The following incremental operating receipts and cash costs are guaranteed under the stipulated funded customer and supplier contracts; no unpaid accrual is omitted.

Incremental two-date operating contract, CU
ItemDate 1Date 2
Revenue and corresponding operating receipts100120
Cash operating costs, excluding taxes and reinvestment6070
Depreciation3030
Additional operating working capitalInvest another 5Recover the entire 15 after operations

The stipulated cash tax is 25% of positive incremental EBIT, paid at the corresponding date. There is no incremental interest, tax shield, later cash flow or separate terminal value. Working-capital recovery is supplied by liquidation and collection of that separate position; it is outside the table's operating receipts. The appropriate discount factors for these guaranteed dated CU cash flows are D(0,1)=9/10 and D(0,2)=4/5. This is one limited corporate investment opportunity, not a maintained cheap quote for an unlimited freely traded claim.

Without the line, legacy operating assets have independently supplied value 100, unrestricted surplus cash is 20 and legacy debt has value 30. That debt is fully secured by a separate legacy asset pool and its value and rights do not change with the line. There are 100 old shares. No other claim exists. Use all 20 of company surplus cash and raise 50 through new ordinary equity from an investor endowed with 60 of actual date-0 cash. The equipment vendor and working-capital supplier receive the resulting 70. The investor receives ordinary ownership in the resulting firm, with the same proportional rights as old shares; no preferred return, refund or additional contribution is promised.

  1. Value the incremental operating decision. Derive both dated FCFFs, the value of the completed line and its date-0 NPV. Explain why depreciation, working-capital recovery and the absence of an extra terminal value matter. Recommend acceptance or rejection under the stated value criterion.
  2. Fund and price the new ownership. Compute status-quo equity value, post-investment equity value, the fair fraction purchased for the new 50, the number of new shares, and old holders' resulting value and gain relative to rejection. Reconcile every recipient of date-0 investment cash and all current claims on the resulting firm. Do not add the used 20 of surplus cash a second time.
  3. A stale issue price. Instead issue the required 50 of new equity at 0.9 per share, the status-quo equity value per old share before incorporating the project. Recompute the newcomer's fraction and value, the old holders' value, and the value transferred to the newcomer beyond its 50 contribution. Does this change the total project NPV? Explain why the status-quo price need not be the fair subscription price after committing to the project.

Case 3 — An investable objective and two return measures

The prospective investor also manages a separately endowed account with 100 CU. In this independent one-period market, a traded growth asset costs ten and pays terminal liquidation cash 18 in U or six in D, with no intermediate dividend. The physical probabilities are one half each. Safe cash has gross return one. No borrowing, shorting, fee, external flow or other asset is permitted in this prospective decision. Invest fraction w∈[0,1] in the growth asset and the remainder in safe cash. The mandate maximizes E[ln(W1/100)], where W1 is terminal wealth. The liquidation payments and safe cash are stipulated funded at that terminal date.

For a separate historical performance question about this manager's account, take two equal one-year periods. It begins with 100; immediately before an external contribution at the end of year 1, its value is 120. The owner then contributes 80 of separately funded cash, so year 2 begins with 200. Ending year-2 wealth is 180, with no other flows or fees. This realized account history is not an assertion that the prospective two-state opportunity repeats through time.

  1. Prove the funded global choice. Write terminal wealth in both physical states, derive the log-utility objective's first and second derivatives, and prove the unique global optimum on [0,1]. Report the actual CU holdings, number of growth-asset units, two terminal wealths and physical expected wealth. State the positivity condition making the logarithms and proof valid.
  2. Price and probability have different jobs. Derive the two strictly positive Arrow prices implied by the growth asset and safe cash. Use them to value the optimal terminal portfolio, and compare that price with physical expected wealth. Explain what changes, and what need not change, if the physical forecast changes while the traded prices and payoffs remain fixed.
  3. Audit the performance claim. Calculate each historical subperiod return, cumulative two-year time-weighted return and annual money-weighted internal rate of return. State and solve the dated cash-flow equation for the latter, restricting the annual gross factor to be positive. Explain why the two returns differ and why neither the 80% increase in account value nor a single favorable time-weighted result establishes investment skill.

Case 4 — A binary operating bonus and a constrained hedge

A separate Juniper contract buys from a hedge trust a European binary claim paying 30 CU at date 2 only if the terminal stock is 144; otherwise it pays zero. Juniper has 20 CU reserved at date 0 to pay the benchmark premium. The claim cannot be exercised early. In the benchmark, stock S0=100 and at each of two equal trading periods it multiplies by u=6/5 or d=4/5. Thus date-1 stock prices are 120 and 80; date-2 prices are 144, 96 and 64. There is no dividend. The borrowing and lending gross factor for each period is 11/10. Fractional positions and all required stock trades are allowed without transaction costs.

The trust receives the claim's replication premium and uses it entirely to establish its hedge. The bank position B is a dated CU asset if positive and an owed CU balance if negative. Stock-sale cash arrives before the corresponding bank and binary-claim settlement. All held stock secures the borrowing and cannot be separately pledged or spent. Controlled sales release title against lender repayment. The secured lender begins with 60 CU of separately available cash. Undrawn lender reserves are held at zero return; accrued loan interest increases its claim but does not arrive as cash before repayment. Stock counterparties have sufficient titled inventory (at least two shares available for these trades) and separately available cash of 200 at the relevant purchase cutoffs. Those funded-market assumptions are part of this finite model, not an audit of an entire economy.

At date 0 and after the date-1 rebalance, debt may not exceed (1−h) times the market value of held shares. The original haircut is h=1/4. The lending agreement permits the advance and controlled stock purchase to settle together against the completed collateral position. There is no separate pre-rebalance margin cutoff, no cash margin account and no further intermediate call before date 2. At date 2, controlled liquidation proceeds pay the secured loan, then the binary claim; any residual belongs to the trust's equity holder.

  1. Derive the finite hedge. Work backward from all terminal states to obtain the claim's value and stock/bank holdings at each date-1 node, then the date-0 holdings and premium. State the local pricing up probability implied by the traded stock and bank account. Verify the terminal claim in every path; no physical probability is supplied or needed.
  2. Show every rebalance is financed. At the up node, calculate the extra shares bought, their cash cost, the bank debt before and after rebalancing, and the lender's actual remaining cash after both advances. At the down node, show how stock sale repays the grown debt. Derive the largest haircut consistent with the original debt/share positions at the monitored dates and verify that h=1/4 is admissible.
  3. Change collateral access at the up node. After reaching S1=120, the permitted haircut becomes 1/3. Keep the binary obligation and required terminal hedge stock holding unchanged. A separate investor has five CU available at that date and may inject actual equity cash, receiving the entire remaining terminal residual after the loan and binary claim; no old shareholder has a duplicate right to that residual. Find the minimum injection, the resulting loan, and the investor's terminal receipts in both remaining states. Check the cash budget and the date-1 value of that new claim. Explain what is established if the investor delivers the cash, and what fails if it merely indicates interest in subscribing.

Case 5 — Gross network payments are not new outside resources

At a separate stress cutoff, two distressed counterparties A and B enter an enforceable simultaneous proportional clearing batch. Incoming batch receipts may finance outgoing batch payments. This is explicitly not sequential gross settlement with an unmodeled intraday credit line. A owes total face 12: one quarter to B and three quarters to an outside treasury bank T. B owes total face 16: one half to A and one half to other outside creditors. All those claims are due in the batch, and there is no fee or interest. External cash already available to A and B is two and three respectively. No other asset can provide batch cash. Every unpaid nominal claim remains recorded after a partial payment.

pA = min(12, 2 + pB/2),   pB = min(16, 3 + pA/4).

T owns all nine of A's outside face claim. Before this stress its stated balance sheet is cash two, that claim carried at nine, and a long asset carried at 20, funded by deposits of 20 and equity 11. In the joint stress, the long asset is marked at 18 and cannot be sold or borrowed against before the deadline. Carry the A claim at its actual clearing receipt under the chosen policy, receive that cash before T's payment, and recognize the impairment once. No recovery of the residual nominal A claim is included in the assessed horizon. T must pay eight of its deposit principal immediately after the batch; the other 12 is due later. When cash is insufficient, pay all available cash and retain the unpaid deposit. There is no automatic insurance, state facility or debt cancellation.

An independent donor has six CU of its own usable cash and actual authority to make irrevocable grants buying no claim or ownership. One permitted route gives x≥0 to A and y≥0 to B before the batch, subject to x+y≤6; replace their external cash by 2+x and 3+y. An alternative route gives cash directly to T before its deposit deadline. Compare the routes under the narrow mandate of paying T's eight on time with the smallest donor outlay. No broader welfare ordering is stipulated.

  1. Clear and reconcile the original batch. Solve the displayed equations, verify the active cap regimes, and prove uniqueness using the maximum absolute coordinate difference between two possible fixed points. Compute each outside group's receipts and reconcile them to the original external cash. Retain the unpaid nominal claims; do not count internal network payments as additional external wealth.
  2. Trace the bank's loss and deadline. Compute T's marked equity before payment, its actual available cash, deposit payment, missed amount and remaining deposit liability. Reconcile the post-payment balance sheet and surviving nominal A claim. Explain why adding A and B's aggregate unpaid faces to T's six-unit claim impairment would not produce a valid further loss for T.
  3. Prove and govern a funded response. Solve the grant-funded clearing system for every x+y≤6 and prove that its caps remain slack throughout that domain. Derive the global minimum total upstream grant that permits T to pay eight, including the allocation, both batch payments and outside receipts at equality. Compare the minimum direct grant to T and identify who receives the difference between the routes. Give a conditional decision under the stated narrow mandate, naming actual funding/delivery evidence, responsibility and one fact or broader objective that would require a new decision.
Form A complete solutions, proofs and scoring

  1. Closing receivables 30, inventory 34, trade payables 23 and unearned advances 14. Receiving the new advance debits cash 12 and credits the customer contract liability 12. Delivering the previously prepaid goods debits that liability eight and credits revenue eight; the associated goods-consumed cost is already part of the supplied 90. The inventory estimate debits write-down expense six and credits inventory six. Receivables are 20+160−150=30. Inventory is 30+100−90−6=34. Payables are 18+100−95=23. Customer advances are 10+12−8=14. Neither cash collection nor a new label is a second sale. Six points: the three correct recognition entries three; all four closing operating balances, with coherent bridges, three.

  2. Income 26, operating cash 33 and closing cash 37 CU. Revenue is 160+8=168. Income is 168−90−6−30−12−4=26. Direct operating cash is 150+12−95−30−4=33. For an indirect check, inventory before the separate write-down would be 40, so its gross increase is ten; receivables increase ten, trade payables increase five and unearned advances increase four. Thus

    CFO = 26 + 12 + 6 − 10 − 10 + 5 + 4 = 33.

    Equivalently, use the net inventory increase of four and omit the extra six add-back: 26+12−10−4+5+4=33. Do not use the net change and add back the same write-down again. Ending cash is 15+33−5−6=37. Net PPE is 80−12=68; debt is 40−5=35. Equity is 77+26−6=97. Closing assets are cash 37 + receivables 30 + inventory 34 + PPE 68 =169. Liabilities are payables 23 + advances 14 + debt 35 =72, giving 169=72+97. The five principal payment removes cash and debt equally; the six dividend reduces cash and equity. Neither is an income-statement operating expense. Eight points: income one; direct CFO one; a valid indirect bridge two; cash and financing classification two; complete assets/liabilities/equity reconciliation two.

  3. The analyst overstates income and equity by 18 CU. Unearned revenue adds 12 too much and the omitted inventory expense adds six too much: reported income would be 44 rather than 26, and closing equity 115 rather than 97. The corresponding errors are an understated customer liability of 12 and overstated inventory of six. The physical receipts and payments do not change: CFO remains 33 and cash 37. A cash-flow statement beginning from the erroneous income needs correction; an erroneous accrual calculation cannot create another 18 of cash.

    Useful evidence includes delivery/acceptance records matched to the opening and new advance contracts, showing when the remaining goods must be supplied; and item-level inventory quantities, sale prices and completion/disposal costs supporting the six write-down. Collection aging and subsequent customer receipts can separately test the credit-sales forecast. CFO exceeding income by seven does not establish recurring earning power: advance receipts create future delivery obligations, payment timing can move cash between periods, and the write-down may reveal deteriorating economics. Full credit accepts other concrete evidence tied to these mechanisms. Six points: quantified income/equity error two; unchanged cash and correct liability/asset explanation two; two specific evidence requests and their forecasting implications two.

  4. FCFF is 65/2 at date 1 and 60 at date 2; line value is 309/4 and NPV is 29/4 CU. Date-1 EBIT is 100−60−30=10; tax is 5/2 and after-tax operating income 15/2. Add noncash depreciation 30 and subtract the extra working-capital investment five to obtain 65/2. Date-2 EBIT is 120−70−30=20, tax five and after-tax operating income 15. Add depreciation 30 and released working capital 15 to get 60. Initial outlay is 60+10=70.

    PV = (9/10)(65/2) + (4/5)60 = 117/4 + 48 = 309/4;
    NPV = 309/4 − 70 = 29/4 = 7.25.

    Depreciation affects stipulated taxable EBIT but is not another cash payment after the equipment purchase. The 15 working-capital recovery is cash returned from a separately funded operating position; it is included once. The line has no remaining equipment value or cash stream, so an added perpetual terminal value would invent an asset. Accept under the stated incremental value criterion, conditional on the supplied contracts and discounting. Seven points: EBIT/taxes and both FCFFs four; coherent dated PV and NPV two; investment recommendation and no-extra-terminal-value scope one.

  5. Fair new ownership is 200/589; old holders retain value 389/4 CU. Rejection gives equity 100+20−30=90. After funding the line, surplus cash is zero and operating assets are worth 100+309/4=709/4. Subtract unchanged legacy debt 30 to obtain post-investment equity 589/4. The investor pays 50 for fair fraction 50/(589/4)=200/589. If n new shares are issued, n/(100+n)=200/589, so n=20000/389, approximately 51.414 shares. Old owners retain fraction 389/589 and value (389/589)(589/4)=389/4=97.25. Their gain over rejection is 97.25−90=7.25, the project NPV.

    The cash allocation at date 0 is exact: the company's available 20 plus the investor's 50 equals the vendor's 60 plus the working-capital supplier's ten. The investor retains ten of its endowed 60 and receives the new shares; no loan principal or new claim on the vendor is invented. Current claim values reconcile as legacy debt 30 + new equity 50 + old equity 389/4 =709/4, equal to the resulting operating assets. The used 20 cash is already in the funded investment and is not a separate surplus asset. Financing allocates the value created by the line; it does not create a second NPV. Eight points: status-quo/post-investment values two; fair fraction and number of shares two; old value and gain two; both cash-recipient and claim-value reconciliations two.

  6. The stale issue transfers 145/56 CU of value to the newcomer. Raising 50 at 0.9 issues 500/9 new shares. Total shares are 1400/9, giving new fraction 5/14 and old fraction 9/14. New value is (5/14)(589/4)=2945/56, approximately 52.589286; old value is (9/14)(589/4)=5301/56, approximately 94.660714. The newcomer's gain is 2945/56−50=145/56. Old owners gain 5301/56−90=261/56. Their sum is (145+261)/56=29/4, the same total NPV. Nothing about the line's productive cash flows changed.

    The fair issue price per share in part (b) is (389/4)/100=389/400=0.9725. The 0.9 status-quo price values rejection and does not allocate the positive project opportunity fairly once commitment and funding are taken into account. This is a comparison of stated issue policies and counterfactual values, not a claim that an informed competitive price would remain stale. Five points: new share count/fraction one; both resulting claim values two; transferred value and conserved NPV one; explanation of the changed valuation basis one.

  7. The unique optimum is w=5/8. Terminal wealth is 100(1+4w/5) in U and 100(1−2w/5) in D. For every w∈[0,1], both are positive; the smaller is at least 60. The normalized objective is

    J(w) = (1/2)ln(1+4w/5) + (1/2)ln(1−2w/5),
    J′(w) = (2/5)/(1+4w/5) − (1/5)/(1−2w/5),
    J″(w) = −(8/25)/(1+4w/5)² − (2/25)/(1−2w/5)² < 0.

    Strict negativity proves strict concavity on the whole feasible interval. Setting J′ to zero gives 2(1−2w/5)=1+4w/5 and hence w=5/8, which lies inside the interval. It is therefore the unique global maximum, not merely a reported stationary point. Invest 125/2=62.5 in the growth asset, buying 25/4=6.25 units, and hold 75/2=37.5 cash. Terminal wealth is 150 or 75; physical expected wealth is 225/2=112.5. The optimum can lose 25 relative to its initial 100 in D. Log utility and these physical probabilities define its objective; expected return alone would select a different policy. Eight points: both wealth functions and positivity two; first/second derivatives two; root and global proof two; funded holdings, terminal wealths and mean two.

  8. Arrow prices are 1/3 for U and 2/3 for D; the portfolio's price is 100 CU. Safe cash gives πU+πD=1. The growth asset gives 18πU+6πD=10. Solving yields πU=1/3 and πD=2/3, both strictly positive. The optimal portfolio costs (1/3)150+(2/3)75=100, matching its funded holdings. Its physical expected wealth is 112.5 because physical probabilities are one half each. The higher mean is exposure to the supplied risk, not 12.5 of arbitrage profit.

    Changing physical beliefs changes the expectation and generally the expected-log optimal fraction. It need not change the quoted Arrow prices or the price of a fixed payoff under the stated market. The price equation uses the traded opportunity set; the preference calculation uses the investor's probability law. Five points: two pricing equations and positive solution two; portfolio price and comparison two; precise forecast-versus-price distinction one.

  9. Cumulative time-weighted return is 8%; the annual money-weighted IRR is zero. Year-1 return is (120−100)/100=20%. The actual 80 contribution starts year 2 at 200; that year's return is (180−200)/200=−10%. Chain the subperiod growth factors: (6/5)(9/10)−1=2/25=8% over both years. If an annualized time-weighted figure is wanted, it is √(27/25)−1; it is not eight percent per year.

    Let g=1+r>0 be the annual money-weighted gross factor. The dated investor flows are −100 at date 0, −80 at date 1 and +180 at date 2, so 100g²+80g−180=0. Factor as 20(g−1)(5g+9)=0. The unique positive root is g=1, hence r=0; the negative root is inadmissible. More of the owner's money was exposed to the losing second year, whereas time weighting chains returns while excluding external flows. The account's 180 versus initial 100 includes an 80 contribution and cannot be labeled an 80% investment return. A single realized path establishes neither a repeatable premium nor manager skill: require a suitable benchmark, matched risk and costs, an untouched evaluation period, and evidence robust to strategy selection and chance. Seven points: both subperiod returns two; cumulative time-weighted calculation one; dated IRR equation, positive root and annual unit two; flow/skill critique with specific evaluation evidence two.

  10. Initial delta is 45/88, initial bank position −4500/121, and premium 3375/242 CU. At any nonterminal node the pricing up weight q solves (11/10)=(6/5)q+(4/5)(1−q), so q=3/4. The bank factor lies strictly between d and u, making both local pricing weights positive. At S1=120, terminal payoffs are 30 and zero. The stock holding is 30/(144−96)=5/8. Its down-state value is 60, so the bank must repay 60 at date 2; date-1 BU=−60/(11/10)=−600/11. Thus VU=(5/8)120−600/11=225/11. At S1=80, both later payoffs are zero, giving VD=ΔD=BD=0.

    The date-0 differences give Δ0=(225/11)/(120−80)=45/88. To make the down-node wealth zero, B0(11/10)=−80(45/88)=−450/11, so B0=−4500/121. Initial cost is 100(45/88)−4500/121=3375/242, approximately 13.946281, below Juniper's funded premium budget 20. Equivalently q²30/(11/10)² gives the same value. At UU, stock 90 less loan 60 pays 30; at UD, stock 60 less loan 60 pays zero. After a first down move the hedge has zero positions and pays zero in DU and DD. The identical terminal stock 96 has the same binary payoff on both paths, although intermediate hedge positions differ. Eight points: local pricing weight one; both date-1 portfolios and values three; initial delta/bank/value three; every path's terminal verification one.

  11. The up-node trade is financed by 150/11 CU of new borrowing. The stock increase is 5/8−45/88=5/44 shares, costing 120(5/44)=150/11. Initial bank debt has grown from 4500/121 to 450/11. Raising it to 600/11 supplies exactly 150/11; there is no unrecorded external hedge cash. The lender's actual cash after the initial advance and the up-node advance is

    60 − 4500/121 − 150/11 = 1110/121 > 0.

    This uses the stated zero return on its undrawn reserve. The accrued interest within 450/11 is a claim, not a receipt available to fund the next advance. At the down node, sale of 45/88 shares at 80 produces 450/11 and repays exactly the grown debt, leaving zero stock, zero debt and zero hedge wealth.

    At date 0, debt divided by collateral value is (4500/121)/[100(45/88)]=8/11. At the up node after rebalance it is (600/11)/75=8/11. Thus both monitored limits require 1−h≥8/11, or h≤3/11. The down-node debt and shares are both zero and require no funding. Since 1/4<3/11, the original haircut works. This test respects the single pledge and stated monitoring times; it does not assume an unmodeled margin call can be postponed. Six points: extra stock and exact financing two; lender cash and interest timing one; down-node cash closure one; both collateral ratios and sharp haircut boundary two.

  12. Minimum new equity is 50/11 CU; it buys the sole terminal residual of five. The required 5/8 shares are worth 75 at the up node. With h=1/3, permitted debt is at most 50 rather than 600/11. The original exact hedge therefore needs replacement cash of at least 600/11−50=50/11. Equality fits the investor's five-CU budget. The grown old loan is 450/11, so additional lender cash is now 50−450/11=100/11. Together with investor cash 50/11 this pays the same 150/11 stock purchase. The resulting date-1 debt is 50; repayment at date 2 is 55.

    After either remaining outcome, stock liquidation minus the original binary claim equals 60: 90−30 in U and 60−0 in D. Paying the loan 55 leaves five for the new equity investor in either state. Its date-1 value is 5/(11/10)=50/11, exactly the injection. That residual has been allocated once; it is not also an old holder's profit. The minimum is sharp: any smaller injection would require debt above 50 while keeping the specified stock hedge. Timely delivered equity makes this revised policy funded, given the stated collateral and settlement rights. An expression of interest supplies no cash and leaves that policy unexecutable. The original benchmark payoff price and the feasibility of a particular borrowing arrangement are separate conclusions; a known future funding change would need an explicit inception contract and evidence. Six points: debt cap and minimum equity two; funded rebalance one; both terminal residuals and their present value two; execution/ownership qualification one.

  13. Total batch payments are pA=pB=4. In the uncapped regime, substitute pB=3+pA/4 into the first equation: pA=7/2+pA/8. Hence pA=4 and pB=4, strictly below their caps 12 and 16; direct substitution proves existence for this contract.

    For uniqueness, let two possible payment vectors have maximum coordinate distance M. The function min(c,z) changes by no more than the change in z. The A equations then differ by at most M/2 and the B equations by at most M/4. Thus M≤M/2, forcing M=0. This proof applies to the supplied open network and simultaneous-clearing rights; it is not a claim about an arbitrary closed cycle or sequential payment system.

    T receives (3/4)4=3 and B's other outside creditors receive (1/2)4=2. Their five exactly uses the original external cash 2+3. Internal transfers are A→B=1 and B→A=2; they support clearing but cancel in the external resource identity. A retains unpaid face eight: two to B and six to T. B retains unpaid face 12: six to A and six to other outsiders. These nominal deficiencies are not extra realized cash. Six points: solution and regime verification two; uniqueness argument two; outside-resource and retained-claim reconciliation two.

  14. T has positive marked equity three but misses three of its deposit payment. Mark the long asset down by two and the nine-unit A claim down to its actual receipt three, a loss of six. Prepayment assets are cash two + claim three + long asset 18 =23 against deposits 20, giving equity three. Collecting the claim exchanges an asset for cash; it does not create another three of revenue or another impairment. Available cash becomes five. Pay five of the eight due and retain the missed three plus the 12 due later: total deposits still owed are 15.

    After paying, assets are the long asset 18, liabilities are deposits 15 and equity remains three. The nominal A claim still unpaid is six, despite its zero remaining carrying amount under the no-further-recovery scenario. A and B's entire unpaid faces include internal and other creditors' claims, and the deterioration transmitted into T's particular claim is already in its six loss. Adding those network faces to T's impairment would mix owners and double count transmission. Six points: separate two/six losses and equity two; actual payment, miss and liability two; post-payment identity and nominal claim one; no-double-counting explanation one.

  15. The cheapest upstream grant is 7/2 to A; the cheapest direct grant is three to T. With funded x,y and both caps slack, solve

    pA = 4 + (8x+4y)/7,   pB = 4 + (2x+8y)/7.

    For x,y≥0 and x+y≤6, pA≤4+8(6)/7=76/7<12 and pB≤76/7<16. These formulas therefore verify an uncapped fixed point throughout the entire permitted grant domain; the same contraction bound proves uniqueness. T receives 3+(6x+3y)/7. Its own two plus that receipt can pay eight exactly when 2x+y≥7. Since 2(x+y)≥2x+y, every feasible upstream response costs at least x+y=7/2. Equality requires y=0 and x=7/2. This lies within the donor's cash budget and yields pA=8, pB=5, T's receipt six and other outsiders' receipt 5/2. Outside receipts total 17/2, equal to external cash five plus donor grant 7/2. Unpaid nominal A and B faces remain four and 11; T's retained nominal A balance is three.

    A direct gift of three to T gives cash 2+3+3=8, the same timely deposit performance. Less cannot fill the original three-CU gap. It leaves the original clearing vector unchanged. Under the upstream route, half a CU more reaches B's other outside creditors (5/2 instead of two), funded by the donor's additional half CU; there is no free aggregate payment multiplier. T ends either successful route with long asset 18, deposits 12 and equity six. With direct support it retains a nominal A deficiency of six; with upstream support that nominal deficiency is three. The supplied horizon assigns no additional recovery to either, so do not manufacture a new asset from the legal face.

    Under the narrow bank-deadline mandate, conditionally choose the three-CU direct grant. Confirm the donor's funded account and actual authority, beneficiary delivery before the cutoff, the clearing batch's legal/netting and payment evidence, T's creditor order and retained balances, and the long asset's unavailability. Treasury owns the delivery/payment record; independent risk challenges the recoveries and duplicate-counting claims; the mandated decision maker records the objective, costs, objections and revision trigger. Evidence that the batch cannot use simultaneous incoming funds, that a stated recovery is unavailable, or that the mandate also protects the other outside creditors requires a new calculation or policy choice. A larger gross network payment alone cannot establish that the more expensive route has higher welfare. Eight points: full-domain solution and cap proof two; global grant bound and equality allocation two; funded direct comparison and recipient difference two; conditional recommendation, execution evidence, responsibility and revision limits two.

Scope of the assessment. All companies, endowments, contracts, probabilities, valuations and numerical examples are original. The linked accepted chapters supply the accounting, finite pricing, utility, replication and institutional-risk methods. No new empirical calibration, current national rule, actual funding commitment or external human certification is asserted. The 300-minute estimate and mastery cutoffs require separate learner evidence; completing this written form alone does not establish the practical, oral or delayed-retention requirements.

The inherited method readings are the scoped MIT accrual-adjustment notes, MIT capital-budgeting notes, dated flow-adjusted return discussion and finite self-financing treatment. The brief governance framing reuses the inspected 2018 stress principles and 2015 governance passages. The numerical proofs and the contractual powers in this examination are original; these readings do not certify reporting compliance, current law or this examination's outcomes.

Form B — Divestment, promises and executable finance

This original reassessment contains five 20-point cases, for 100 points. Suggested time is 300 minutes, an uncalibrated design target. Use a nonprogrammable calculator and blank paper; no notes, internet or code. All required numerical inputs appear below. Keep exact fractions where practical, state units, and show the reason for each journal, value, constraint and decision. The authored advancement standard is at least 85 overall and 15 in every domain, followed by an unfamiliar transfer and teach-back. A critical accounting, identification, funding, units, double-counting or integrity error requires remediation regardless of the total. This is not a credential or an empirically equated examination.

The cases follow fictional Briar Engineering, a related investment mandate, its commodity hedge and a lending bank. They are separate, fully specified decision snapshots, not one continuous set of financial statements. Each restates the resources and rights it needs. Do not import cash, debt or a permission from another question. CU is the single fictional currency unit. Physical probabilities are labeled P; pricing weights and probabilities are labeled separately. No current market quote, national reporting rule, statutory priority or actual funding commitment is asserted.

Question 1. Two estimates cannot manufacture a receipt — 20 points

Briar begins a year with cash 12, gross trade receivables 30 less allowance 2, inventory 24 and net equipment 80. Liabilities are trade payables 20 and debt 70; equity is 54. During the year it earns cash revenue 16 and credit revenue 90, collects 84 from receivables, buys inventory for 36 entirely on trade credit, pays suppliers 32, consumes inventory costing 40 and pays other operating expenses 20. There is no other transaction, tax, interest, distribution or financing flow.

At the start of the year, genuinely new engineering evidence changes the equipment's estimated remaining life from six years to four, retaining residual value 8. Past entries were correct when made. Apply straight-line depreciation prospectively to the opening carrying amount. After the full year's depreciation, independent evidence establishes recoverable amount 50 for this independently cash-generating equipment. Apply the stipulated cost-model rule: impairment equals the positive excess of carrying amount over recoverable amount; there is no upward revaluation. At year-end the required total receivable allowance is 5. There are no writeoffs or recoveries. These are supplied measurement conventions and evidence, not a conclusion about an actual filing's compliance.

  1. (a) Give the depreciation, impairment and allowance-adjustment entries. Compute profit and the complete closing balance sheet, including cash and equity. Reconcile both sides. Explain why neither a contra-asset balance nor an impairment charge is a cash reserve.
  2. (b) Derive operating cash flow directly and indirectly. Show one indirect bridge using gross receivables and a second using net receivables. A spreadsheet uses the net-receivable change and also adds the allowance expense: quantify its error and explain it.
  3. (c) A controller proposes retaining the old six-year estimate to “raise this year's profit by six.” Compute the counterfactual depreciation and impairment while retaining the independently established recoverable amount 50. Assess the claim, the prospective-treatment issue and the evidence needed before changing an estimate. Does the numerical reconciliation validate that evidence?

Question 2. A valuable restructuring can still need creditor consent — 20 points

In a new decision snapshot, a division carried at 50 can be sold immediately for 64 to a buyer with that much available cash. Transfer of control and cash is simultaneous; the seller pays a disposal-service provider 3 immediately. Alternatively the division delivers certain unlevered distributable cash 20 at date 1 and 44 at date 2. The latter includes all final disposal proceeds; there is no remaining asset. These cash flows are already net of every relevant operating and investment outlay. The compatible date-0 discount factors for certain cash are 0.95 and 0.90. There is no tax. Debt service is a financing allocation, not an additional deduction inside these operating cash flows.

For parts (b) and (c), the sale has been selected and completed. Only the following incremental restructuring scope remains. Net sale cash is 61. An old creditor has principal face 70, with no further interest; its contract requires all available sale proceeds to repay principal immediately, reducing the remaining face one-for-one. The rest is due at date 2. The retained core produces final distributable cash 50 in state U and 10 in state D. Supplied strictly positive date-0 state prices for those date-2 receipts are 0.45 and 0.45; they sum to the stated date-2 discount factor. They are not physical default probabilities.

A proposed rehabilitation consumes 25 cash immediately and changes the retained core's final cash to 90 in U and 30 in D. All required work is included in that expenditure; there is no later funding need or other asset. Releasing 25 from the cash sweep requires the creditor's explicit consent. In that proposal only 36 is repaid as principal now. At date 2 the creditor receives the smaller of its remaining face and core cash; existing equity receives the residual. An unpaid nominal debt claim remains recorded, but there are no further assets, guarantors or recoveries in this closed scope. Its economic value after the final distribution is zero; no legal discharge is presumed.

The existing owners also have five CU of personal cash, separate from all corporate resources. They may pay a consent fee f directly to the creditor now. The fee is a separately agreed transfer and does not reduce remaining principal. It conveys no new equity rights. Unpaid personal cash remains theirs. Both parties use the supplied pricing rule to compare present values; the creditor accepts weakly equal value. Their only alternatives here are the contractual cash sweep without rehabilitation or the stated rehabilitation with an affordable fee. No compulsory restructuring power is available.

Question 3. A feasible investment mandate need not fund every liability — 20 points

A separate employee reserve has 100 CU now and must pay a date-1 liability of 90, 100 or 110 in states L, M and H. A default-free cash investment costs one and pays one. Only cash and the risky asset are traded. Do not infer complete markets from the existence of three states or from the supplied vector.

The reserve begins entirely in cash. Buying n risky units incurs an additional execution fee 0.02n, paid now to an outside execution provider. Fractional units are allowed. The remaining b CU stays in the cash investment. No shorting or borrowing is permitted, and 0≤n≤30. The first mandate is deliberately limited: maximize P-expected terminal surplus over the liability, subject only to covering the liability in L. It does not require full coverage in M or H. No sponsor contribution is currently authorized.

For part (c) only, a separate sponsor can instead transfer a nonrepayable g≥0 before investment from an independently funded one-CU cash budget. The sponsor receives no claim; unused sponsor cash remains outside the reserve. The reserve then invests 100+g under the same cost and position restrictions. No other mechanism changes the liabilities.

(d) A sales presentation reports a 14% gross annual return from the best of twenty inspected historical windows and calls the part (b) allocation “fully immunized.” Give a concise evidence-based response addressing selection, the mandate and the cash required for a valid full-coverage decision. Method and evidence scope. The cases, amounts, state laws, contracts and rubrics are original. For the taught methods, revisit estimate changes and impairment, receivable and inventory rollforwards, restructuring and claimant participation, positive state prices and traded spans, investment mandates, dated forwards and futures cash, and funding and collateral availability. The source record preserves the accepted, actually inspected primary scopes behind those methods; it does not certify the hypothetical estimates or legal rights.

Specific dated anchors are the March 2021 AASB 108 compilation, paragraphs 32–40 for prospective estimates and December 2022 AASB 136 compilation, paragraphs 59–63 for the stipulated impairment method; Lo's MIT capital-budgeting lectures for incremental value; World Bank 2021 Principles for informed workouts as policy guidance, not domestic authority; Brunnermeier's finite pricing lecture; CFA Institute's May 2010 institutional-policy guidance; Haugh's 2016 forwards/futures notes and the 11 June 2015 CME variation-calculation document; and the September 2008 Basel liquidity principles and July 2015 governance principles. No current reporting compliance, clearing rule, supervisory threshold or legal permission is inferred from these historical and methodological references.

Integrated practical: Morrow's production order and Cedar's client promises

This open-resource project asks one question: may a reserve institution finance a productive order while meeting its own dated promises? A positive project NPV, a profitable accounting period and a positive expected portfolio surplus are three different pieces of evidence. You must connect them through actual ownership and cash. The supplied implementation is an instructor benchmark; submit your own equations and code before consulting it.

Suggested work: 10–14 hours plus a 20-minute defense, not a calibrated completion-time norm. Prerequisites are the accepted finance core in Volumes 7–11. This practical samples reconciled accounts, claim valuation, mandate-constrained allocation, credit protection, settlement and governance. It does not examine every detail of all 60 chapters, estimate empirical probabilities or certify professional practice. Every institution, CU amount, legal right, price and probability below is an original teaching assumption.

1. One contract, three terminal cutoffs

Morrow Components has a legacy operating business and owns an exclusive new production opportunity. A separate project company, or SPV, will undertake it. Cedar Reserve may buy part of the SPV's note. Cedar has already received 57.6 CU of client prefunding and 6.4 CU of sponsor equity: its opening cash is 64, not an unfinanced promise of future support. It owes clients 20 at 09:00 and 44 at 12:00 on terminal day T. All three cutoffs below are on that same day, not three years. The discount from entry t0 to any T cash is 0.9; intraday carry is zero. The difference between noon and 16:00 still matters because a deadline is a contractual constraint.

Event order; a receipt listed first is usable before that cutoff's payment
TimeEvents and limits
Before t0Close Morrow's historical accounts and pay its remaining trade payables. Retain at least 10 of parent operating cash. Existing protection pools and their separately owned claims are already funded.
t0Client and sponsor pay Cedar; note and equity subscriptions pay the SPV; the SPV pays for equipment and inventory. Cedar buys an existing protection claim, pays fees and buys bills with all remaining cash.
T, 09:00The bill issuer pays Cedar. Cedar then pays up to the first client obligation of 20 from actual available cash.
T, 12:00The SPV's customers pay, the equipment buyer pays, operating costs are paid and the note/equity waterfall executes. Timely escrow protection pays. Cedar then pays up to the second client obligation of 44.
T, 16:00The credit-exposed protection estate pays. A delayed escrow transfer, if explicitly imposed, also arrives now. Cedar uses cash to cure overdue client claims before retaining capital. A cure does not erase the noon breach.

All accounts use CU. There is no tax, transaction interest within T, short sale, cross-entity cash sweep, implicit overdraft, client deposit insurance or emergency credit. Parent and SPV property are separate. A reserve floor is a decision test, not a claimant inserted ahead of clients. A missing payment remains a nominal claim; assigning zero additional modeled recovery does not legally cancel it. All customer receipts and the equipment purchase are stipulated funded external payments at 12:00. Their payers' full balance sheets, the legacy parent's later debt service and the wider economy are outside the conservation claim.

The new SPV buys equipment for 30 and inventory for 20 at t0. It consumes all inventory, depreciates equipment by 20 and sells the remaining equipment for its book value of 10 at T. It pays other operating costs of 30 at noon. Sales are fully collected then; there are no ending operating receivables, inventory or additional taxes. The parent contributes its pre-existing exclusive opportunity, with zero book carrying amount, and receives the residual ownership not sold to the new equity subscriber. Its opportunity has economic value; this is not extra cash in the project account.

A state price buys one terminal CU only in that state. Price a terminal claim by π·X, not P·X. The strictly positive prices sum to 9/10, matching the unit bill. The normalized pricing probabilities are (2/9, 1/3, 4/9); they are not the supplied physical probabilities. The reference pricing market permits the long and short positions needed for payoff comparisons. Cedar's own mandate does not: a reference-market replication is not automatically an executable reserve strategy.

The SPV issues one zero-coupon note of face 50. It pays min(50,V), where V is available project cash after operating costs and the equipment sale. Shareholders receive max(V−50,0). The note is senior only to this SPV's residual equity; it has no claim on the parent's retained operating cash. Price the note and equity first. Sell enough equity at its correctly priced value to complete the 50 cash investment after the note proceeds. For the stated book illustration, initially record the note at its issue proceeds and accrete the discount to face before final repayment. Record no automatic forgiveness of an unpaid face claim.

3. What Cedar can buy, and who funds each payment

A separately endowed underwriter buys whatever fraction of the note Cedar does not buy. It has 50 cash. A new equity subscriber has 20 cash. The sponsor has 10 cash before paying 6.4; the client payer has 60 before paying 57.6. The bill issuer has 100 cash before receiving Cedar's bill subscription; its redemption is funded from these resources. An equipment seller and inventory supplier receive the original investment cash. No provider's unspent money is available to Cedar without a new contract.

An existing dealer owns one whole unit of each protection claim below before t0. Cedar buys a fraction from that dealer, not a newly written fraction of an underfunded promise. The dealer keeps every unpurchased fraction, including the whole unselected claim. Each unit's aggregate claim is fixed. Purchase prices go to the dealer; they do not top up either protection pool. The pools were separately endowed before t0 and cannot be pledged twice or used to pay the SPV's operating costs.

Existing protection claims, per whole unit
ClaimRight, priority and paymentEntry price and implementation cost
EscrowIn the down state, a nominal capped claim of 20 against a segregated 20 cash pool, paid before the noon client deadline. Other states pay no claim. Idle pool cash returns to its writer at noon. Baseline: no prior claim.Price 4; custody/execution fee 0.4 per unit additionally paid to an independent service provider.
Credit-exposedIn the down state, the same nominal capped claim of 20, but only a separately funded estate of 12 is available at 16:00. All holders share it pro rata; unpaid nominal rights total 8. Other states pay no claim, and idle 12 returns to the writer at 16:00.Price 12/5; no additional custody fee.

The cap remains 20 if the SPV's down-state cash later deteriorates. These are defined contingent contracts, not universal reimbursement of every note loss. No priority, custody rule or timing assumption is borrowed from current national law. Documentary failure is a scenario below. Until the stated return time, writers' idle pool cash is unavailable to them and to Cedar. Even when released, it is their cash, not an authorized reserve facility.

Cedar's note purchase incurs an execution fee of 0.1 per whole note in addition to its price. It chooses note fraction x from {1/2, 3/4, 1}. For each x it chooses exactly one of five protection actions: none; credit-exposed h=x/2 or h=x; escrow h=x/2 or h=x. Thus the complete menu has 15 policies. It cannot mix the two protection claims. Invest all remaining cash B in bills at 0.9 per terminal unit. There are no other fees or trades.

The mandate is to hold at least half the production note, pay both client deadlines in every supplied state, and retain terminal net capital of at least 2 in every state. Net capital is remaining cash minus any surviving client arrears, after actual late cures. Among qualifying policies maximize P-expected terminal net capital. Exact ties favor lower x, then lower h, then the alphabetically earlier claim label. The parent cash gate must also pass for the integrated approval. The minimum production allocation and the 2 capital floor are board choices, not regulatory ratios or universal investment advice.

Baseline and before-trade comparisons select a prospective funded entry policy. After a revenue, priority or delivery shock is discovered after entry, actual holdings remain the baseline half-note/quarter-escrow position. Comparing the other 14 policies then asks what would have survived had it been chosen at the original entry tickets. Such a historical-entry counterfactual supplies no unwind price, refund, rebalance cash or authority to switch now. The output labels this distinction and tests actual post-trade approval against the unchanged holdings. A change only to physical probabilities is a new prospective assessment, with the same market prices.

Report risk relative to the terminal net cash-only benchmark K₀=64/(9/10)−64, even though cash-only violates the production mandate. Define loss L=K₀−K. Report its physical mean, left 90% quantile and worst 10% average including only the needed fraction of a probability atom. Negative loss means outperformance of this stated benchmark. Risk reports do not replace either payment deadline.

4. Learner submission and decision standard

Submit a decision memo of at most 1,800 words, a rights-and-cash map, a reconciled calculation appendix, your source/input evidence register, executable standard-library code with a quiet function and documented domain, strict JSON results, and a correction log. Include a reproducible command from a directory other than the code's own directory. Record at least one initially plausible answer that your reconciliation rejected. Separate independent calculations from copied benchmark output. The code should enumerate this small menu; no simulation, library installation or generic trading platform is needed.

  1. D1 — Operating accounts. Reconstruct income, direct and indirect operating cash, all closing balances and the post-payables cash gate. Explain which evidence would verify sales recognition, receivable collection and the timing of supplier payment. Show why a balanced journal alone is insufficient evidence of correct recognition.
  2. D2 — Investment and ownership. Derive statewise project cash, note/equity payoffs, values and incremental NPV. Complete the issue proceeds, new equity ownership and retained parent opportunity value. Reconcile book equity, shareholder distributions and surviving note claims. Account for all funded entry subscriptions and all recipients of the final SPV cash.
  3. D3 — Mandate and selection. Enumerate all 15 funded policies, derive the feasible set and prove the selected policy is optimal in it. Distinguish physical expected capital, price, initial sponsor capital and fee-adjusted economic value. Calculate the selected policy's specified loss, VaR and ES with an atom-correct proof.
  4. D4 — Hedge and settlement. Prove the baseline escrow payoff's reference replication and price. Reconcile protection ownership, separate pools, all receipts, client payments, arrears and cures at 09:00, 12:00 and 16:00. Explain why a late recovery with a positive terminal surplus can fail the institution's mandate. Derive the fixed-position reverse capital boundary and its information-timing qualification.
  5. D5 — Institutional decision and evidence. Recommend approval, conditional revision or refusal, with named evidence owners, authority, cutoffs and stop conditions. Identify whose resources and residual wealth finance the strategy and whose nominal claims survive in rejected states. Deliver meaningful independent checks and defend at least one unfamiliar transfer below without consulting its answer.
100-point rubric; numerical work and interpretation both matter
Essential domainPointsAllocation
Accounting and cash evidence20Income and two CFO routes 7; complete balance sheet and payment gate 7; evidence and recognition critique 6.
Value, financing and rights20Cash/payoff/value derivations 6; proceeds/ownership/book distinction 7; funded sources and every SPV recipient 7.
Portfolio decision20Complete funded menu 5; feasible-set and optimality proof 6; physical-versus-pricing and fee interpretation 4; atom-correct loss measures 5.
