The authored mastery rule is at least 85/100 and at least 15/20 in every domain, followed by a successful unfamiliar transfer and teach-back. These are design thresholds, not institutionally accredited standards. Critical errors require repair and reassessment regardless of total: using physical probabilities as prices without a pricing model; treating face value as issue cash; financing a purchase from an unreceived or another entity's payment; double counting a pool or equity contribution; erasing an unpaid right; recording expected cash as executed cash; or concealing benchmark dependence. A defensible refusal because legal or operational evidence is absent can earn full decision credit even though the stipulated numerical baseline is feasible.

5. Instructor benchmark: reconstruct before judging

D1 — Two cash routes and the parent's gate

Income is 100−60−20−10=10. Direct operating cash is 90−55−20=15. Closing receivables are 20+100−90=30; inventory 30+50−60=20; payables 20+50−55=15. Indirect operating cash is 10+10−(30−20)−(20−30)+(15−20)=15. The subtraction of a negative inventory change adds 10; the reduction in payables uses 5.

Closing assets are cash 25, receivables 30, inventory 20 and equipment 50, totaling 125. Payables 15, old debt 40 and equity 70 also total 125. Paying the remaining 15 trade payables leaves cash 10, exactly the retained operating floor. That payment is not a second expense. The new SPV does not supply this cash. The conclusion is this narrow operating gate, not a valuation or solvency opinion on the entire legacy parent.

Inspect sale contracts and delivery/acceptance evidence for recognition; match customer remittances and bank receipts to individual receivables; match supplier invoices, inventory receipts and dated payment instructions. A fictitious sale debits receivables and credits income in balance while overstating both assets and earnings. An early supplier payment can be arithmetically correct but violate an assumed cash date. Independent external evidence and the stated recognition convention therefore matter beyond debit/credit equality.

D2 — One investment, several claims

Operating income is (−20,10,40). Final unlevered cash is sales−30+10=(30,60,90): the inventory was paid at t0 and cannot be subtracted a second time from terminal cash. Equivalently add depreciation 20 and the 20 inventory expense already paid at t0 (subtract the inventory change of −20), then collect the equipment sale 10. This inventory adjustment is not an extra inventory-sale receipt. Project value is (1/5)30+(3/10)60+(2/5)90=60, so incremental NPV is 10.

The note pays (30,50,50), price 41. Equity pays (0,10,40), price 19. Their state payoffs and prices add to the project's; subtracting face 50 from enterprise value 60 gives the wrong equity value of 10. Debt proceeds 41 leave 9 of new cash equity to raise. The outside subscriber receives 9/19 of residual equity; the parent keeps 10/19, worth 10. An exclusive opportunity can explain that retained value while contributing no spendable CU to the SPV. The pre-existing parent opportunity owner bears its own opportunity cost; it is not an unexplained windfall created by the financing journal.

Initial book assets are 50, debt carrying value 41 and contributed book equity 9. Accreting the 9 discount produces pre-resolution income (−29,1,31) and book equity (−20,10,40). In the down state, the estate pays the note 30 and leaves a nominal unpaid claim of 20; the contractual shareholder payout is zero. A negative pre-resolution book residual is neither a negative shareholder distribution nor permission to delete the creditor. The modeled estate has no further recovery, but the nominal claim survives. The normal/up debt payoff is 50, and all residual equity cash goes to the two owners in their fractions.

At the chosen x=1/2, Cedar and the underwriter each pay 41/2 for the note; the equity subscriber pays 9. These cash sources total 50, paid as 30 to the equipment seller and 20 to the inventory supplier. The underwriter retains 59/2 cash; the subscriber retains 11. At T, Cedar/underwriter each receive (15,25,25); the outside equity holder receives (0,90/19,360/19); the parent receives (0,100/19,400/19). Each state's receipts add exactly to (30,60,90). In the down state each note holder separately retains a nominal unpaid claim of 10. The parent's legacy reserve of 10 is never in this waterfall.

Let k be the protection label, h its whole-claim fraction, and ak its price. Fees are f=0.1x+0.4h for escrow and f=0.1x otherwise. Bill purchase is B=64−41x−akh−f. Terminal net capital, including any retained client debt, is Ks=B/0.9+xNs+hHk,s−64. This terminal identity is useful for the objective, but only the separate execution ledger proves each deadline.

Here is a proof that enumeration did not miss a better allowed policy. No hedge yields down-state noon net cash (64−141x)/9; even x=1/2 makes it negative. Buying a credit claim reduces bills further and supplies no noon receipt. Thus all six credit policies and three unhedged policies fail a deadline. Half escrow h=x/2 gives down capital (64−73x)/9. Requiring at least 2 means x≤46/73, so only x=1/2 qualifies. Full escrow h=x produces state-independent capital (64−5x)/9, decreasing in x; all three menu values meet the floor. The best fully protected policy has capital 41/6. The partially protected x=1/2,h=1/4 has expected capital 281/36, higher by 35/36. This proves the unique optimum among the four feasible policies. It proves nothing about a different mandate, a continuous menu or unlisted states.

The selected bills cost 847/20. Fees of 3/20 are real outflows: note execution 1/20 and custody 1/10. Its down capital is 55/18 and other-state capital 145/18. Initial sponsor capital is 32/5; terminal expected capital is 281/36. Price-weighted residual capital is 25/4, equal to 64−3/20−288/5. The liability PV of 288/5 is justified for these supported full-performance policies, not as the fair value of a rejected policy's defaulting client claim. Do not add expected surplus to a market value or call the fee a payment to the SPV.

The cash-only benchmark is 64/9. Selected losses are (73/18,−17/18,−17/18), with mean −25/36. The left 90% quantile is −17/18 because that loss has probability 19/20. The worst 10% includes all 1/20 down mass and 1/20 of the other-state atom, so ES0.9=[(1/20)(73/18)+(1/20)(−17/18)]/(1/10)=14/9. Averaging only the observations strictly above VaR would report 73/18 and would not be this ES. The fully protected half-note has positive benchmark loss 5/18 in every state: protection improves the worst state but costs expected capital under the stipulated physical law.

D4 — Replication, actual execution and a reverse boundary

On the three supplied states, 50 terminal bill units minus one note pay (20,0,0). Their cost is 50(0.9)−41=4, exactly the escrow claim's frictionless quote. A timing-matched reference bill can pay at noon; with zero intraday carry its stated price equals the 09:00 bill's, and a 09:00 receipt can be held until noon. The payoff basis consisting of bill, note and equity has determinant 600, so it spans these three states. Neither this spanning nor the cost cancels Cedar's short-sale prohibition, custody fee, or the escrow delivery condition. The credit-exposed payoff is (12,0,0) at 16:00, priced 12/5; the earlier deadline remains a separate restriction.

A revealing rejected policy is x=1/2 with full credit protection h=1/2. Its down terminal net capital is 71/18, above the 2 floor, but its noon cash is only 755/18. It misses 37/18 of the 44 payment; a late receipt of 6 cures the gap and leaves 71/18. Neither positive capital nor that cure makes the original noon payment punctual.

For a down-sales loss δ learned after entry, keep historical purchases and the selected holdings fixed. Project cash falls by δ, Cedar's note recovery by δ/2, and the capped protection remains 5. Hence Kdown(δ)=55/18−δ/2 on 0≤δ≤10. The capital test holds exactly through δ=19/9, with equality included; full noon client payment lasts through δ=55/9. The capital floor fails first. This is a fixed-position boundary, not the best response over the menu. If the information is known before entry, the note price and equity subscription must change; the corresponding boundary is derived in Transfer 2. A compound priority or settlement change invalidates the single-shock certificate rather than merely adding a new label to it.

D5 — A conditional institutional decision

Under every supplied baseline fact, approve the SPV's funded issue and Cedar's x=1/2,h=1/4 escrow strategy. Morrow's retained cash is exactly 10; Cedar pays every deadline and retains more than 2 in every state. State the narrow scope: the legacy debt's later service, states outside the table and the external counterparties' true financial condition have not been established. Do not approve a larger allocation solely because its expected capital is higher; the unhedged whole-note score 94/9 accompanies a real default.

The controller owns recognition and bank-statement reconciliation. The financing officer verifies the entire 50 cash subscriptions, issue price and equity register before spending. Treasury verifies bill redemption and actual receipt identifiers, custody segregation, the noon escrow release condition and the exclusive allocation of each pool. Risk independently challenges the down revenue, pricing/physical distinction, cap and omitted catastrophe state. An authorized committee approves the finite mandate and any bridge as a new contract; an operator cannot create authority by editing the model. Stop execution if entry funds, delivery priority or payment instructions are unverified. Report a deadline failure even after its cure, together with the amount, cause, claim identifier and corrective owner.

Require two-person confirmation of custody and payment evidence, reconcile dealer and Cedar unit ownership to one, and test the model against an independent payoff equation and transaction ledger. Preserve input hashes, code version, changed assumptions and rejected hypotheses. Reward correct escalation and accurate failure records, not a quiet terminal balance. These controls are reasoned design proposals, not estimated prevention probabilities. A counterparty attestation, a pricing quote, and a successful unit test answer different questions; none alone proves timely cash delivery.

The instructor should accept an explicitly funded and authorized alternative only as a changed contract, then grade its complete revised cash and rights rather than silently enlarging the baseline menu. If the student's independent code disagrees with the benchmark, require a minimal reproducible contract and reconciled recipients; do not award points merely for matching a saved JSON file.

6. Six unfamiliar transfers

Use these after the learner submits the baseline. The first five are supported input interventions except the explicitly new bridge. The sixth changes the state space and is a separate analytical extension. The examiner chooses at least one without advance answer access; assign remediation by the affected domain, not a second automatic 100-point score.

  1. Collections, not earnings. Keep recognized historical sales at 100 but receive only 80 from customers. Rebuild the closing accounts and payment gate. May the SPV's fully subscribed 50 repair the parent's position without another transaction?
  2. When did the information arrive? Let only down-state customer cash and sales fall by δ, with 0≤δ≤10. First suppose the change arrives after all baseline subscriptions. Derive the old selected position's capital boundary, then evaluate δ=5/2 and identify the best qualifying historical-entry counterfactual in the menu; no current switch is funded. Next suppose the same revenue information is known before any subscriptions; reprice the note, issue enough equity at fair value, and recompute bills, ownership, the fixed-position boundary and the optimal entry policy. Keep the cap, fees, dates, state prices and physical probabilities fixed.
  3. A different physical assessment. Change P to (3/10,3/10,2/5) without changing state prices, cash or contracts. Recompute the decision. Holding the two favorable states' combined mass at 1−p, derive the exact down-probability switch between the baseline selected policy and full half-note escrow protection. Explain equality.
  4. Delivery after the deadline. After entry, escrow becomes available only at 16:00. Show the old selected policy's noon payment and late cure; check the entire original menu. Then consider a newly authorized interest-free intraday bridge from a provider with its own 2 cash: find the minimum advance before noon and show its 16:00 repayment and remaining provider cash. This bridge is outside the original runtime menu.
  5. An adverse custody finding. After entry, discover a genuine senior claim of 5 against the escrow pool, payable first at that pool's settlement time in every state. Remaining pool cash serves the down-state hedge claims pro rata; idle residual returns to the writer in other states. Keep historical ticket prices. Recompute the actual old selected policy, the best historical-entry counterfactual, and every recipient of the pool under each. Explain why the comparison does not authorize a switch, and distinguish the historical-price loss from a before-trade fair-price question.
  6. A catastrophe outside the model. Replace the three states by four project estates (10,30,60,90), while the bill, note and equity prices remain (9/10,41,19). The note still has face 50. A capped protection pays (20,20,0,0). Derive every strictly positive state-price vector consistent with those traded prices, the protection's admissible price interval and its endpoint exclusions. Supply explicit lower/upper hedges. Do not invent a catastrophe probability.
Transfer 1 — A cash gate can fail while income stays positive

Income remains 10, but CFO becomes 80−55−20=5. Closing cash is 15, receivables 40, inventory 20 and equipment 50: assets still total 125. Payables 15, debt 40 and equity 70 remain unchanged. Indirect CFO is 10+10−20+10−5=5. Paying all payables leaves cash zero, a 10 gap to the operating floor. The SPV's 50 belongs to its contracted investment; diverting it would leave that purchase unfunded and change the note/equity rights. The model may still select the same reserve policy while refusing integrated approval because the separate parent gate fails. Remedies require actual new funds or an explicitly redesigned operating/investment contract, not another recognition entry.

Transfer 2 — Historical subscriptions and fair new subscriptions differ

After trade, note entry proceeds stay 41, new equity cash stays 9 and ownership stays 9/19 versus 10/19. Only actual down recovery and current marks change. The old partial policy has K=55/18−δ/2; its inclusive floor boundary is 19/9. At δ=5/2 it has 65/36, so it fails the 2 floor even though clients are paid. The best qualifying historical-entry counterfactual is x=h=1/2 escrow, with down capital 67/12, other-state capital 41/6 and expected capital 325/48. Those purchases would have worked if chosen originally; no supplied transaction converts the actual partial position to them now. Actual post-trade approval therefore fails pending a separately funded repair.

Before trade, project value is 60−δ/5 and note price is 41−δ/5. Total equity value stays 19 because the down equity payoff is already zero. New cash equity is 9+δ/5, with fraction (9+δ/5)/19; the parent retains value 10−δ/5. The selected partial position saves δ/10 on its note purchase and earns δ/9 more terminal bill cash, while losing δ/2 of note recovery. Thus Kdown=55/18−7δ/18 and the inclusive fixed-position floor boundary is 19/7. This is not the after-trade 19/9 boundary.

At δ=5/2 the note costs 81/2, project value is 119/2, new equity cash is 19/2 and each equity owner holds 1/2. The old partial position now buys bills for 213/5, retains 82/3 after the first client payment, and ends with down capital 25/12 and other capital 25/3. Its expected capital is 385/48; it still qualifies and is the best of the recomputed 15 policies. In both information contracts the unpaid down note face is 45/2, split by note ownership. Lower price improves a new buyer's funding; it cannot retroactively give cash back to an old holder. Neither conclusion licenses changing the protection's capped 20 payoff.

Transfer 3 — A probability change need not reprice a claim

With down probability 3/10, the old partial policy's mean is (3/10)(55/18)+(7/10)(145/18)=59/9. Full half-note protection still yields 41/6 in every state and is now optimal; other fully protected menu entries yield less. Every statewise feasibility result, entry quote and ownership fraction is unchanged. For general down probability p, the partial mean is 145/18−5p. Equality with 41/6 occurs at p=11/45. Below this value choose partial protection; above it choose full half-note protection. At equality the stated tie rule chooses h=1/4. The split between the two favorable-state probabilities does not affect this comparison because their note and hedge cash coincide. These are conditional decisions under stipulated P, not evidence that markets must share the committee's probabilities.

Transfer 4 — Same terminal wealth, a different obligation record

For the old selected position, down-state cash before the noon client payment is 487/18+15=757/18. It pays that amount, missing 35/18. At 16:00 the escrow receipt of 5 cures the 35/18 and leaves 55/18. Every original policy fails the down noon deadline: even the cheapest unhedged half-note lacks enough cash, and either kind of protection reduces bills while contributing no earlier receipt. A positive final balance is therefore insufficient.

An authorized bridge of exactly 35/18 before noon restores timely payment for the old position. Its provider starts with 2=36/18, retains 1/18 while the loan is outstanding, and receives 35/18 back from the late escrow receipt, restoring its 2. Cedar retains 55/18 after that repayment. Any smaller bridge leaves a noon shortfall. The new loan and its repayment are balance-sheet claims, not income or shareholder contributions. The equality uses zero bridge interest and certain authorized access by the cutoff; fees, interest, senior recourse or failed execution would require a new calculation. The baseline code correctly reports no qualifying policy because this facility was not in its menu.

Transfer 5 — A prior right changes available collateral

The senior holder receives 5 from the 20 pool first, leaving 15. In the down state the actual old partial holder receives 15/4 rather than 5; the dealer receives 45/4. Their nominal unpaid hedge rights are 5/4 and 15/4. Down capital falls to 65/36; other-state capital stays 145/18, giving mean 1115/144. Clients are paid but the capital floor fails. Full half-note escrow is the best historical-entry counterfactual: down capital 13/3, other capital 41/6 and mean 161/24. Full three-quarter protection also qualifies but has a lower mean; full whole-note protection has down capital 14/9 and fails. No unwind or new hedge purchase is provided, so this comparison is not an executable post-discovery switch.

Under the counterfactual half-unit escrow holding the pool would pay senior holder 5, Cedar 15/2 and dealer 15/2 in the down state, with aggregate unpaid hedge rights of 5 split as 5/2 each. In the other states, either holding pays the senior holder 5 and returns 15 to the writer, with no triggered hedge claim. The separate credit pool is unchanged and never fills the escrow gap. If known before a new trade, the delivered escrow cash would have state-price value 3; the stipulated discovery after payment instead leaves a historical purchase at 4 and a loss to its holders. The runtime deliberately rejects combining its revenue-only before-trade contract with this priority discovery.

Transfer 6 — An open incomplete-price interval

The note pays (10,30,50,50), equity (0,0,10,40). Let the first state price be t. Solving the bill, note and equity price equations gives π(t)=(t, 1/5−2t, 3/10+4t/3, 2/5−t/3). All components are strictly positive exactly when 0<t<1/10. Conversely every such vector prices the three securities correctly, so this is the full family. The claim price is 20[π₁(t)+π₂(t)]=4−20t, hence the open interval (2,4). At t=1/20 the vector is (1/20,1/10,11/30,23/60) and the claim costs 3. No physical probability is implied.

The subhedge 25 bills minus one-half note costs 2 and pays (20,10,0,0), no more than the claim. The superhedge 50 bills minus one note costs 4 and pays (40,20,0,0), no less than the claim. At a claim price of 2, buy the claim and sell the subhedge for zero entry cash; the resulting payoff is (0,10,0,0). At price 4, buy the superhedge and sell the claim for zero cash; the payoff is (20,0,0,0). Both are nonnegative with a strictly positive payoff in a possible state. Thus either endpoint contradicts the reference market's no-arbitrage assumptions with these unrestricted comparison positions. Positive interior prices are attainable by the displayed pricing family. The original three-state replication pays too much in the new catastrophe state, so it is no longer an exact hedge. This is a constructive finite proof, not a general continuous-time completeness claim or an executable short position authorized for Cedar.

7. Defense, reassessment and scope

Teach-back. In two minutes explain why 10, 19, 41, 50 and 60 can all be correct in the same project, and why a positive final reserve can coexist with a client breach. A complete explanation identifies respectively incremental opportunity value, residual-equity value, note proceeds, initial cash investment or note face (two different uses), and project value; it connects each to its dated cash or claim. It then uses the late-protection ledger, rather than a slogan, to show the missed deadline. The listener should be able to identify who pays each number.

Delayed retention. After 7–14 days, hide the table and reconstruct the selected down capital from its four t0 purchases and two client payments. Correct reconstruction is 64−20.5−0.05−1−0.1=42.35 invested in bills; 42.35/0.9−20+15+5−44=55/18. Then explain why deleting the fee, pooling the two writers' estates or moving a 16:00 receipt to noon changes the contract. Repeat the failed domain with a new timing or ownership transfer and an updated correction log. This protocol measures the submitted performance, not a guaranteed long-term competence result.

For remediation revisit statement reconciliation and debt book versus market value; claim-consistent free cash flow; finite-state pricing and investment mandates; incomplete prices and contingent rights; and loss atoms, dated funding and controlled decisions. This small case omits tax, stochastic continuous-time hedging, estimation error, legal adjudication, endogenous prices and whole-economy equilibrium. These omissions delimit the inference; they do not become zero risks in a real institution.

8. Reproducibility and source boundaries

Download original inputs, benchmark Python, baseline results, standalone instructions and the four-file manifest. Keep the four payloads together. The default command python3 /absolute/path/finance-core-analysis.py is quiet and writes the neighboring output file. An explicit --input INPUT --output OUTPUT works from another directory; python3 -O has the same behavior. Importing the file and calling run(data) is quiet, does not mutate its argument and returns strict JSON-safe data.

The model supports exactly three states and 15 policies, collections in [80,90], a down-sales loss in [0,10], strictly positive physical weights summing exactly to one, the two stated escrow cutoffs and a discovered senior claim in [0,5]. Other structural terms are deliberately fixed. Before-trade information reprices revenue only and cannot be combined with a discovered priority or delay. Each decimal's reduced rational denominator must be at most 1012; this is a denominator bound, not a count of decimal places. Exact rational arithmetic determines decisions. JSON rejects duplicate keys, nonfinite values, booleans as numbers and undeclared fields. Direct, resolved-path, symlink and hardlink aliases to inputs or protected payloads are refused before any output write. The separate checker reconstructs economic equations and uses focused counterfactuals; a manifest proves byte identity, not financial truth or actual settlement.

The methodological links below reuse the library's previously inspected primary scopes; no new current standard or fresh empirical observation is asserted. All numbers, transactions, proofs, prompts and solutions here are original.

  • SEC, 2007 financial-statement guide: dated introductory statement connections; not a current accounting rule. MIT, 2003 debt lecture: face, issue proceeds and book/market distinctions.
  • Damodaran's FCFF/FCFE definitions: claim-consistent cash and noncash working capital; unrelated ratio and tax generalizations are not adopted.
  • Brunnermeier's one-period pricing notes: linear state prices and completeness. CFA Institute, May 2010 institutional policy statement guide: objectives, responsibilities and liquidity constraints; no compliance claim or borrowed numerical limit.
  • Haugh's 2016 discrete pricing notes, single-period completeness sections: an extension route; the four-state family and endpoint hedges above supply this project's proof.
  • Rockafellar and Uryasev, general loss distributions: atom-adjusted tail definitions. BCBS, September 2008 liquidity principles: dated access and collateral framing, as international guidance rather than national authority.

Oral transfer and teach-back · 20 points

After the written and practical work, explain each changed contract without consulting its answer. Allow approximately twenty minutes for all five prompts; this is an uncalibrated guide. Each is worth four points. Require at least 17/20 and three points in every item, with any critical error remediated. The grader should ask which observation would change the conclusion, rather than rewarding fluent repetition.

  1. A new label on an old asset. An analyst proposes to fix a company’s missed payment by reclassifying a late receivable as a current asset and reversing its allowance. Its contractual collection date, collectible amount and account access have not changed. Explain the separate accounting, value and cash questions, the evidence that could justify an estimate revision, and what would actually repair the deadline.
  2. The forecast changes, the traded prices do not. A one-date operating asset pays 120/60 CU in U/D. Traded Arrow prices remain 0.3/0.6, but the analyst changes the physical U probability from 0.8 to 0.2. Compute the change in expected asset payoff and explain whether the supplied market value changes. Describe an additional fact that would justify revaluation.
  3. Fund the implementation cost. An investor has 100 CU, must pay a two-CU fee immediately from that cash, and can allocate the remaining amount without shorting between assets with physical mean returns 6% and 10%. The mandate requires expected final wealth at least 108, with no later contributions or borrowing. Is the target feasible? State the exact resource calculation and a transparent revision the decision maker could consider.
  4. A previously omitted state. A stock costs 80 CU; the one-period bank gross return is one. Stock outcomes 100, 80 and 60 are all possible. Only the stock and bank account are traded, with fractional long/short positions permitted. A call pays max(S−80,0). Explain why the half-share/30-CU debt hedge valid at the extreme outcomes fails in the middle. Construct strictly positive state prices consistent with the traded assets and characterize the call values they permit.
  5. Approval is earlier than delivery. A payment needs five CU at 10:00. There is no available cash. A separately funded lender signs an irrevocable five-CU facility at 09:00, but the contract and payment system deliver funds only at noon. There is no other borrowing or deferral right. State what the signature establishes, what it does not establish, the actual deadline outcome, and the evidence needed for a different feasible plan.
Oral answers and scoring criteria
  1. An asset’s classification does not change its collection date or turn a carrying value into cash. An allowance revision needs evidence about recoverable amount under the applicable stated recognition policy; unchanged evidence does not justify an opportunistic reversal. Even a justified upward value revision would not pay the earlier obligation. Repair needs an actual funded sale, timely advance or contribution, or an effective change in the obligation’s due date, with the new cost, recourse and rights recorded. Credit four: classification/cash distinction one; evidence-based estimate revision one; actual dated repair one; new claims/costs and authority one. Merely reporting higher equity earns no funding credit.
  2. The physical expected payoff falls from 0.8(120)+0.2(60)=108 to 0.2(120)+0.8(60)=72 CU. The supplied traded-price value remains 0.3(120)+0.6(60)=72 in either forecast. Equality between the new physical mean and the price is a numerical coincidence, not a pricing principle. Changed claim payoffs, traded state prices, enforceability or access could require revaluation; a different physical forecast alone does not override the stipulated replicating prices. Credit four: both means one; correct unchanged price one; distinct roles/coincidence one; concrete revaluation evidence one.
  3. Only 98 can be invested. A long-only mixture’s mean return cannot exceed 10%, so maximum expected final wealth is 98(1.10)=107.8 CU, a net expected return of 7.8% on the original 100. The 108 target is infeasible even before considering risk. The decision maker could reduce the target, negotiate a lower funded fee, supply new capital with explicit performance accounting, or authorize a different opportunity set and reassess its risks. None is silently included in this mandate. Credit four: investable amount one; global maximum argument one; exact shortfall/return one; explicit rather than hidden mandate revision one.
  4. Half a share less debt 30 pays 20,10,0 while the call pays 20,0,0, so the middle-state error is ten CU. Any stock/bank payoff is affine in S; the two extreme equations uniquely select that failed middle value, proving nonreplication. Let state prices be a,1−2a,a. They sum to one and price the stock at 100a+80(1−2a)+60a=80; strict positivity requires 0<a<1/2. The corresponding call value is 20a, ranging over the open interval (0,10). These are positive pricing extensions, not a unique selected price or an assertion that all investors agree. The endpoints would require a zero state price despite all three states being possible. Credit four: middle-state error one; nonreplication argument one; valid positive price family one; range and nonuniqueness one.
  5. The signature establishes the promised contractual advance under the stated terms, not beneficiary cash at 10:00. The actual first-cutoff cash is zero and the five-CU payment is missed. Noon receipt cannot undo that history. A revised plan needs demonstrable earlier usable delivery, a distinct funded bridge with its own repayment, or an effective agreed deadline change. Check who owns the money, the account/location and authorization, timestamps, settlement finality and later obligations. Credit four: commitment/delivery distinction one; actual failure one; funded or authorized alternative one; concrete evidence and later claims one.

Delayed retention · 50 points

After 14–21 days, attempt these five new cases without notes or the solutions, allowing about ninety minutes. These timing and spacing suggestions are authored study choices. Each case is worth ten points; require 43/50 overall and at least eight in each case. If a mechanism fails, reconstruct it from the relevant chapter, explain the correction, and solve a newly changed contract before a later retry. A remembered final number is not sufficient.

  1. Allowance and the cash bridge. Under a stipulated teaching accounting policy, revenue is 130 CU and receipts are 110. Gross receivables begin at 20 and end at 40; the allowance begins at zero and a new provision of six creates an ending allowance of six. There are no charge-offs. Cash operating costs are 60 and depreciation is ten. There are no taxes, financing interest or other accruals. Opening cash is ten, capital expenditure is 25, new borrowing is five and dividends are 15. Derive net receivables and income. Reconcile operating cash both using the change in gross receivables and using the change in net receivables. Compute FCFF under these zero-tax/no-interest assumptions and closing cash. Explain the tempting double count and distinguish the provision from an actual payment.
  2. A financed acquisition of contingent claims. An operating opportunity delivers 120/60 CU at the sole terminal date. Strictly positive traded Arrow prices are 0.3/0.6, respectively. A particular investor can negotiate one acquisition for an outlay of 62; this is a limited opportunity, not a claim that 62 is a maintained no-arbitrage quote for freely traded identical assets. A new, fairly priced senior debt claim has face 80, actual recovery min(80,operating payoff), no recourse elsewhere and no transaction costs. Equity receives the residual. The debt buyer has 70 CU of separately available cash and the investor has five CU; their unspent cash stays outside the acquired operation. The acquisition uses debt proceeds plus the investor’s own contribution, and has no other cash balance. Compute operating value, debt proceeds, equity value, the investor’s required contribution and its NPV. Show statewise and present-value conservation and reconcile the unspent funding. Explain why physical U probability 0.8 does not justify raising debt proceeds to its expected face payment.
  3. A constrained allocation has a different optimum. Two assets have mean one-period returns 0.06 and 0.10 and covariance matrix [[0.01,0.005],[0.005,0.04]]. Weights are w and 1−w; there is no shorting, borrowing, contribution, fee or cash holding. Derive portfolio variance and prove its global minimum over 0≤w≤1. Compute the mean at that minimum. Now require portfolio mean at least 0.08. Determine the entire feasible weight set and its minimum-variance member, including its variance. Explain why changing the mandate changes the solution without changing the covariance estimates, and identify a limitation of treating the supplied estimates as known future risks.
  4. The hedge pays correctly but needs margin. A stock costs 80 CU and ends at 100 or 60, with no dividend. A zero-rate bank account and unrestricted fractional positions give a frictionless call with strike 80 a replication cost of ten: buy half a share for 40 and borrow 30. Consider a seller who receives the ten-CU base premium and uses it entirely for that replication. The bank has separately funded the 30-CU loan at inception. Before maturity it requires five CU of segregated cash margin; it cannot lend or spend that collateral, pays no interest on it, and returns all five before final loan/option settlement. The seller has no other cash. A distinct lender has five CU available, can advance the margin shortfall before its cutoff, and receives gross repayment 1.04 after collateral return. The seller may additionally charge x CU at inception and retain it as cash for margin, with 0≤x≤5; the buyer has separate available cash of 15 and this is a proposed private quote, not an assertion of a competitive equilibrium. Verify the base hedge in both states. Trace the margin and bridge when x=0, then derive the smallest x leaving nonnegative terminal seller cash in both states under this fixed policy. Explain why this amount is a policy-specific funding break-even charge, not a universal no-arbitrage option price.
  5. The FX hedge’s recovery arrives late. A company begins with four H and collects a 20-F invoice before a 36-H supplier payment is due. At the stipulated stressed spot rate one H per F, a dealer with twenty H of separate available cash buys all twenty F before that cutoff. The company already holds a cash-settled short-20-F forward struck at two H per F; its contractual positive payoff is twenty H. Zero inception premium was a contractual assumption, not evidence of fair counterparty-risk pricing. On counterparty default, three H of its separately posted collateral is controlled, transferred and usable before the supplier cutoff. The remaining unsecured claim is seventeen H and recovers 50%, but only after that cutoff; this recovery excludes the collateral. No other cash arrives. A bridge provider has nine H available before the cutoff and requires repayment at gross factor 1.05 after the late recovery. A separate donor has one H of available cash and may make an irrevocable nonrepayable grant g∈[0,1] before the supplier cutoff, buying no claim. Compute ultimate forward recovery, early payment gap, and the late deficit with a bridge alone. Derive the minimum grant and corresponding bridge that pay every stated obligation on time; prove necessity and sufficiency. Do not count collateral twice or erase the bridge’s interest.
Retention solutions, proofs and rubrics
  1. Net receivables 34; income 54; operating cash 50; FCFF 25; closing cash 25 CU. Gross receivables reconcile as 20+130−110=40. The provision reduces net receivables to 40−6=34 and income to 130−60−10−6=54. It is an expense/allowance entry, not a cash disbursement. Using gross receivables, operating cash is 54+10+6−(40−20)=50. Using net receivables instead, it is 54+10−(34−20)=50. The latter change already incorporates the six-unit allowance increase, so adding the provision again would incorrectly produce 56. Direct receipts less paid costs, 110−60=50, provide an independent check. With the explicitly zero tax and financing interest, FCFF is operating cash less capital expenditure, 50−25=25. Ending cash is 10+50−25+5−15=25. Debt issuance and dividends belong to financing; the new allowance is neither a receipt nor a source available to fund either. Credit ten: receivable and income values two; both valid bridges three; double-counting explanation two; FCFF one; closing cash and classification two.
  2. Operating value 72; debt proceeds 60; equity value 12; own cash two; investor NPV ten CU. In U, 120 is allocated as debt 80 and equity 40; in D, 60 goes to debt and equity gets zero. Operating value is 0.3(120)+0.6(60)=72. Debt raises 0.3(80)+0.6(60)=60, rather than its promised face 80. Equity is worth 0.3(40)+0.6(0)=12, and 60+12=72 matches the priced operating resources. The seller receives the negotiated 62, funded by lender proceeds 60 and investor cash two. The lender retains ten of its original 70, while the investor retains three of its five outside the acquisition. The new claim values plus those unspent amounts are 70 for the lender and 15 for the investor, preserving the lender’s wealth and giving the investor the stated ten-CU gain. Investor NPV is 12−2=10, equivalently operating value 72 less acquisition cost 62. The financing division has not created another ten of total value. Under physical U probability 0.8, the debt’s mean payment is 0.8(80)+0.2(60)=76 and mean operating payoff is 108; neither is its current price. The debt’s default-contingent payoff and the supplied state prices determine its proceeds. Positive NPV describes this available acquisition under the stated market and access assumptions, not proof that such an opportunity persists in a frictionless competitive market. Credit ten: both actual state allocations two; three coherent values three; funded contribution and NPV two; face/expectation/price distinction two; opportunity-scope limitation one.
  3. Unconstrained minimum w=7/8; constrained minimum w=1/2. Variance is 0.01w²+0.04(1−w)²+2(0.005)w(1−w)=0.04w²−0.07w+0.04. The covariance matrix is positive definite: its first diagonal entry is positive and determinant is 0.000375=3/8000>0. Completing the square gives V(w)=(1/25)(w−7/8)²+3/320. The unique global minimum lies within [0,1], at w=7/8 with variance 3/320=0.009375. Its mean is 0.1−0.04(7/8)=13/200=0.065. The target 0.1−0.04w≥0.08 is equivalent to w≤1/2, so feasible weights are [0,1/2]. On that entire interval V′(w)=0.08w−0.07 is negative; hence the unique constrained minimum is its right endpoint w=1/2, variance 3/200=0.015 and mean 0.08. The more demanding expected-return mandate excludes the former solution. Estimated means/covariances can shift, especially in stress; the calculation is conditional and says neither that realized return meets the target nor that estimation error has been priced away. Credit ten: variance derivation two; global minimum proof and variance two; mean one; complete feasible set two; constrained optimum/variance two; estimation/realized-return limitation one.
  4. The additional break-even charge is 5/26 CU, approximately 0.192308. Half a share returns 50 or 30; repaying the original zero-rate loan 30 leaves 20 or zero, exactly the call obligation. At inception, base premium ten plus that original loan thirty funds the forty-CU share purchase. There is no residual base-premium cash. With x=0 the separate bridge delivers five, all of which is posted as margin. Its return of five precedes the bridge repayment of 5(1.04)=5.2, so the seller loses 0.2 despite correct derivative replication. The margin principal is not a trading expense, and the original thirty-CU loan has not disappeared.

    With additional cash x, the seller posts x+(5−x)=5 and borrows only 5−x from the distinct provider. This is between zero and five and fits that provider’s endowment. After the original hedge/option payments cancel in each state, remaining seller cash is 5−1.04(5−x)=1.04x−0.2. Thus nonnegative terminal cash is equivalent to x≥0.2/1.04=5/26. Equality is feasible: the bridge is 125/26, its repayment is exactly five, and all collateral return is allocated once. The buyer pays 10+5/26=265/26, below its supplied cash 15. Every smaller x produces a terminal funding loss under this same policy. This is a private break-even condition given asymmetric funding, the imposed collateral process and the decision to retain the extra charge. It is not a replacement for the frictionless replication theorem, a claim that the quote is competitively accepted, or a universal option price across traders with different funding access. Credit ten: original two-state hedge two; dated margin/bridge path two; shortfall at x=0 one; sharp charge with necessity/sufficiency three; private-policy versus market-price scope two.

  5. Minimum grant 19/21 H and bridge 170/21 H. The forward’s ultimate collected amount is collateral three plus unsecured recovery 0.5(20−3)=8.5, totaling 11.5 H. Its original twenty-H claim is not fully paid. The dealer actually supplies twenty H for the invoice’s twenty F, using its separate twenty-H endowment. Before the supplier cutoff, only 4+20+3=27 H is usable, so the gap is nine. A bridge of nine pays the supplier, but repayment later is 9(1.05)=9.45 against late cash 8.5, leaving a deficit of 0.95 H. Even ultimate unfinanced cash, 4+20+11.5=35.5, is below the supplier’s 36; timing is not the only problem.

    For any early grant g, the smallest bridge that can pay the supplier is b=9−g. Taking a larger bridge would increase later interest and cannot improve final feasibility: if b exceeds that minimum, the unused early cash carries, and final cash is 27+g+b−36+8.5−1.05b=g−0.5−0.05b. The first-date constraint b≥9−g therefore implies final cash≤1.05g−0.95. Necessity is g≥0.95/1.05=19/21. At equality choose b=9−19/21=170/21, which is below the provider’s nine-H capacity; the grant is below the donor’s one-H capacity. The supplier receives exactly 36 at its cutoff, with zero company cash left. Late recovery 8.5 equals 1.05(170/21), so the bridge is paid in full and final cash is zero. The donor supplies the grant from its own endowment and receives no reimbursement; it is not another disguised loan. This proves feasibility of all named company obligations in the supplied state, not the counterparty’s default frequency or the forward’s fair inception price. Credit ten: recovery base and total two; early cash gap one; bridge-only late deficit two; global lower bound on grant two; equality with dated cash and provider budgets two; scope one.

From a wrong answer to a new capability

Keep a correction log with four entries: the exact failed proposition, the violated account or assumption, a reconstructed derivation, and the result of a fresh transfer. Useful routes are accruals and earnings quality for retention 1; acquisition economics and state prices for retention 2; constrained allocation and execution costs for retention 3; collateral funding and replication for retention 4; and credit recovery, funding and cross-border claims for retention 5. Change the binding assumption—collection date, recovery priority, investment constraint or funding term—before claiming that the original error is repaired.

Where the connected arguments are taught

  • From transactions to a forecast: double entry, long-lived assets, financing obligations, ownership, relevant costs, business ratios, linked forecasts, comparability and forensic integration.
  • From operating choices to value: incremental investment, terminal economics, financing frictions, liquidity and payout, comparables, flexibility, private financing, restructuring and capital allocation.
  • From return evidence to an investable mandate: equilibrium pricing, factors, predictability, performance evaluation, dynamic allocation, illiquidity and investment policy.
  • From ideal hedges to qualified model use: rate sensitivity, term-structure measures, stochastic calculus, diffusion replication, hedge sensitivities, numerical error, incompleteness and model governance.
  • From a claim to institutional performance: intermediation, tail risk, operational and legal evidence, long-horizon promises, regulation and incentives, systemic transmission and risk governance.

What passes from the finance core into graduate work

An accounting identity disciplines what can be claimed about a company. A valuation model states which future claims are priced and under what assumptions. A portfolio decision chooses exposures subject to an investor’s objectives and resources. A hedge redistributes state payoffs and creates its own financing and execution needs. An institution must actually perform the resulting obligations within its authority. None of these steps can substitute for the others.

The next task is to assess how such models meet evidence. Advanced econometrics separates the object of interest from what a dataset identifies and what an estimator computes; graduate theory develops the assumptions behind equilibrium and incentive arguments; graduate macro-finance connects household, firm and intermediary decisions over time. Preserve the habits practiced here: exact units and dates, explicit information sets, funded decisions, reproducible calculations and conclusions limited by their evidence.

Passing this package demonstrates performance on its supplied tasks under the recorded conditions. It does not establish every frontier result, universal examination success, legal authority, investment returns or an institutional appointment. The library’s complete production plan remains separate from the chapters and assessments already written and reviewed.
